**Surat Yusuf (The Chapter of Joseph)**

(Surat Yusuf, peace be upon him, is Meccan [[Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is Meccan, except three verses at its beginning. Al-Qurtubi transmitted from them: except four verses. See: al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/277; al-Qurtubi: 9/118.]])

﷽ (In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

* *

﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ That is, its lawful and unlawful matters are clear, and its limits and rulings are clear. Qatadah said: "Mubin (clear), by God, means its blessing, its guidance and its rightness; so this is from *baana*, meaning it became apparent."

Al-Zajjaj said: "*Mubayyin* means it distinguishes truth from falsehood and lawful from unlawful; so this is from *abana*, in the sense of *azhara* (it made clear)."

﴿Indeed, We have sent it down﴾, meaning the Book, ﴿as an Arabic Qur'an that you might understand﴾. That is: We sent it down in your language, so that you may know its meanings and comprehend what is in it.

﴿We relate to you﴾, that is, We recite to you ﴿the best of stories﴾. The *qass* (narrator of stories) is the one who follows the traces and brings the report in its proper form.

Its meaning: We explain to you the reports of the earlier nations and the bygone generations in the best explanation.

It was also said: the intended meaning is specifically the story of Joseph, peace be upon him, which He called the best of stories because of the lessons, wisdom, subtle points and benefits it contains that are fit for both religion and worldly life: the conduct of kings, slaves and scholars, the cunning of women, patience over the harm of enemies, the goodness of forgiving them after reconciliation, and other benefits.

Khalid ibn Ma'dan said: "Surat Yusuf and Surat Maryam are what the people of Paradise delight in within Paradise."

Ibn 'Ata' said: "No grieving person hears Surat Yusuf without finding relief in it."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿By what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an﴾. Here "ma" is a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: by Our revelation to you. ﴿And indeed you were, before it, among the unaware﴾, that is, before Our revelation you were among those who were heedless of this story and did not know it.

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may God be pleased with him, said: "The Qur'an was sent down upon the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he recited it to them for a time. They said: 'O Messenger of God, if only you would relate to us (a narrative).' So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿God has sent down the best of speech﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. They said: 'O Messenger of God, if only you would tell us stories.' So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. They said: 'O Messenger of God, if only you would admonish us.' So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God?﴾ [al-Hadid: 16]."

[[Narrated by al-Tabari: 15/55; Ibn Hibban authenticated it, p. 432 of Mawarid al-Zam'an; al-Hakim: 2/345, and al-Dhahabi agreed with him; al-Wahidi transmitted it through him in Asbab al-Nuzul, p. 311. It was also narrated by Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh. See: al-Durr al-Manthur: 4/496; al-Matalib al-'Aliyah: 3/343.]]

**The commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verse 4:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When Joseph said to his father﴾. That is: "And remember when Joseph said to his father." Yusuf (Joseph) is a Hebrew name [that was Arabicized] [[Omitted from manuscript "B".]], and for this reason it is not inflected [by ʿiʿrab (grammatical case endings)]. It is also said that it is an Arabic name [[Omitted from manuscript "B".]].

Abu al-Hasan al-Aqta' was asked about Yusuf. He said: "*al-asaf* in the language means sorrow, and *al-asif* means the servant. Both meanings came together in Yusuf, peace be upon him, so he was named after them."

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliki informed us, Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il said: Abd Allah ibn Muhammad said: Abd al-Samad narrated to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn Dinar, from his father, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, the noble one, son of the noble one, son of the noble one, son of the noble one, is Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in the chapter on the stories of the prophets, under the verse "Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers are signs for those who ask" (6/419); and in the Tafsir of Surah Yusuf, under "and complete His favor upon you" (8/361); and also in al-Manaqib. Muslim narrated it in abridged form. The author also cited it in Sharh al-Sunnah (13/126). See: al-Silsilah al-Sahihah of al-Albani (4/152).]].

﴿O my father﴾. Abu Ja'far and Ibn Amir read ﴿Yā abatā﴾ with a fatha on the ta' throughout the Qur'an, on the reckoning of: "Yā abatāh (O my father!)."

The others read ﴿Yā abati﴾ with a kasra on the ta', because its original form is *yā abat*, and the final sukun is moved to a kasra.

﴿Indeed I saw eleven stars﴾, that is, eleven stars among the stars of the sky. The word *kawākib* (stars) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz).

﴿And the sun and the moon—I saw them prostrating to me﴾. He did not say "I saw them (feminine) prostrating to me," and the hā', mīm, yā' and nūn here are pronouns used for rational beings, because when He reported about them with a verb used for rational beings, He referred to them with a pronoun used for rational beings, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [al-Naml: 18].

In interpretation, the stars were his brothers, and they were eleven men who were guided by, just as the stars are used for guidance. The sun was his father, and the moon was his mother. This is the view of Qatadah.

Al-Suddi said: the moon was his maternal aunt, because his mother Rahil had died.

Ibn Jurayj said: the moon was his father and the sun was his mother, because *al-shams* (the sun) is feminine and *al-qamar* (the moon) is masculine.

Yusuf, peace be upon him, was twelve years old when he saw this vision.

It is also said: he saw it on the night of Friday, the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr). Then, when he related it to his father...

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verse 5:**

﴿He said, "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers."﴾ This is because the visions of the prophets, peace be upon them, are revelation. Ya'qub knew that when the brothers heard it, they would envy him, so he commanded him to keep it secret. ﴿Lest they devise a plot against you﴾, meaning they would scheme to destroy you, because they know its interpretation and would envy you. The lam in his words "lak" (against you) is redundant (ṣila), like His words, exalted is He: ﴿for their Lord they fear﴾ [al-A'raf: 154]. It was also said that it is like the expression "nasahtuka" and "nasahtu laka" (I advised you), and "shakartuka" and "shakartu laka" (I thanked you).

﴿Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾, meaning: Satan embellishes these things for them and drives them to scheming, because of his ancient enmity.

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliḥī informed us: Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Shurayh informed us: Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi informed us: Ali ibn al-Ja'd informed us: Shu'ba informed us, from Abd Rabbihi ibn Sa'id, who said: I heard Abu Salama say: "I used to see visions that worried me, until I heard Abu Qatada say: 'I used to see visions that made me ill, until I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "The good vision is from Allah, the Exalted, [and the dream is from Satan]. [[Omitted in manuscript "A".]] So when one of you sees what he loves, let him not relate it except to someone he loves; and when he sees what he dislikes, let him seek refuge in Allah from its evil and from the evil of Satan, spit three times, and not relate it to anyone, for it will not harm him."'" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Ta'bir, chapter "The good vision is one part of forty-six parts of prophethood": 12/373; Muslim at the beginning of the Book of Visions, no. (2261): 4/1772; and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 12/206.]]

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliḥī informed us: Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Shurayh informed us: Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi informed us: Ali ibn al-Ja'd informed us: Shu'ba informed us, from Ya'la ibn Ata, from Waki' ibn Adas, from Abu Razin al-Uqayli, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The vision is one part of forty, or forty-six parts, of prophethood, and it stands on the foot of a bird. When it is related, it falls." And I think he said: "Do not relate it except to a beloved one or a discerning one." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud in al-Adab, chapter "The vision": 7/298-299; al-Tirmidhi in al-Ru'ya, chapter "What has come concerning the interpretation of visions": 6/558-559, and he said: "This is a ḥasan (good) ṣaḥīḥ (sound) ḥadīth." Ibn Majah in Ta'bir al-Ru'ya, chapter "The vision, when interpreted, falls...", no. (3914): 2/1288; al-Hakim authenticated it: 4/390, and al-Dhahabi agreed with him; Imam Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad: 4/10; and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah said: "This is a ḥasan ḥadīth": 12/213. His words "on the foot of a bird" are a simile, and its meaning is that it does not settle in its place as long as it is not interpreted. As for relating it to a beloved one, that is because he will only face you in its interpretation with what you love; and the discerning one will inform you of its reality or of the closest thing that can be known about it.]]

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 6:**

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you﴾, meaning your Lord will select you. Ya'qub said this to Yusuf. That is, just as He raised your station through this dream, so your Lord will select you. ﴿And teach you the interpretation of events﴾, meaning the interpretation of dreams. It is called *ta'wil* (interpretation, lit. "return to an outcome") because the matter returns to what he saw in his sleep. *Ta'wil* is that which returns to the final outcome of a matter. ﴿And complete His favor upon you﴾, meaning through prophethood. ﴿And upon the family of Ya'qub﴾, meaning upon his children, for all of his children were prophets. ﴿Just as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq﴾, by making them both prophets. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾.

It was also said: the completion of the favor upon Ibrahim was *al-khullah* (intimate friendship with God), and upon Ishaq it was his deliverance from the sacrifice [[This is according to the view that the one to be sacrificed was Ishaq, peace be upon him, but the sound and established position is the opposite. For this reason we place here a comprehensive passage from Ibn al-Qayyim and his teacher Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on them both, which refutes the view that the one to be sacrificed was Ishaq. Ibn al-Qayyim said in *Zad al-Ma'ad* (1/71–75): "As for the view that it was Ishaq, it is false for more than twenty reasons. I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God sanctify his spirit, say: this view is only derived from the People of the Book, and it is false even by the text of their own scripture. In it, God commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice his son, his firstborn, and in another version, his only son. The People of the Book and the Muslims do not doubt that Isma'il was his firstborn. What deceived the proponents of this view is that in the Torah in their hands it says: 'Sacrifice your son Ishaq.' He said: this addition is from their distortion and lies, for it contradicts his saying: 'Sacrifice your firstborn and your only son.' But the Jews envied the sons of Isma'il for this honor, and wished it for themselves, and to attribute it to them, and to take it for themselves to the exclusion of the Arabs. But God refuses except to give His grace to its people. How can it be said that the sacrificed one was Ishaq, when God gave good news to his mother of him and of his son Ya'qub? God the Exalted said regarding the angels, that they said to Ibrahim when they brought him the good news: (Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lut. And his wife was standing, and she laughed. So We gave her good news of Ishaq and after Ishaq, Ya'qub) (Hud: 70–71). It is impossible that He would give her good news that she would have a son, and then command his sacrifice. There is no doubt that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, is included in the good news. The good news concerning Ishaq and Ya'qub is one wording, and this is the apparent meaning and context of the speech. If it is said: if the matter were as you have stated, then 'Ya'qub' would be in the genitive as a conjunction to Ishaq, and the reading would be 'and after Ishaq, Ya'qub' in the genitive, meaning 'and Ya'qub after Ishaq.' It is said: the nominative does not prevent Ya'qub from being the one given good news of, because the good news is a specific statement, and it is the first true, pleasing report. God the Exalted's saying 'and after Ishaq, Ya'qub' is a sentence containing these conditions, so it is good news; indeed, the reality of good news is the informative sentence. Since good news is speech, the position of this sentence is in the accusative by way of quoting speech, as if the meaning were: 'And We said to her: after Ishaq, Ya'qub.' When one who says 'I gave good news to so-and-so of the arrival of his brother and his baggage following him' is understood to have given good news of both matters together, this is something no person of understanding can doubt at all. Another matter also weakens the genitive reading, which is the weakness of your saying: 'I passed by Zayd and after him 'Amr.' The conjunction stands in place of the preposition, so it is not separated from the genitive noun, just as the preposition is not separated from the noun it governs. It is also indicated that when God the Exalted mentioned the story of Ibrahim and his sacrificed son in Surat al-Saffat, He said: (So when they had both submitted, and he put him down upon his forehead, We called to him, 'O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision.' Indeed, that is how We reward the doers of good. Indeed, this was the clear trial. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice. And We left for him among later generations: Peace upon Ibrahim. Thus do We reward the doers of good. Indeed, he was among Our believing servants) (al-Saffat: 103–111). Then God the Exalted said: ﴿And We gave him good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 112]. This is good news from God the Exalted to him, as thanks for his patience with what he was commanded. This is very clearly, indeed like an explicit text, that the one given good news of is other than the first. If it is said: the second good news was about his prophethood, meaning that when the father was patient with what he was commanded, and the son submitted to God's command, God rewarded him by giving him prophethood. It is said: the good news was about the whole: his person and his existence, and that he would be a prophet. For this reason, 'a prophet' is in the accusative as a predicated state (*hal muqaddar*), meaning: his prophethood being determined. So it is not possible to exclude that the good news falls upon the essence, then to restrict it to a subordinate, ancillary state that functions as an adjunct. This would be an absurdity of speech. Rather, if the good news falls upon his prophethood, then its falling upon his existence is more appropriate and more fitting. Also, there is no doubt that the sacrifice took place in Makkah, which is why the sacrificial offerings on the Day of Sacrifice were made there, just as sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah and the stoning of the pillars (*ramy al-jimar*) were made a reminder of the matter of Isma'il and his mother, and an establishment of the remembrance of God. It is known that Isma'il and his mother were the two who were in Makkah, not Ishaq and his mother. For this reason, the place and time of the sacrifice are connected to the Sacred House, whose building was shared by Ibrahim and Isma'il, and the slaughter in Makkah was part of the completion of the Hajj to the House, which was by the hand of Ibrahim and his son Isma'il, in time and place. Had the sacrifice been in Syria, as the People of the Book claim, and those who took from them claim, the offerings and slaughter would have been in Syria, not in Makkah. Also, God the Exalted named the sacrificed one *halim* (forbearing), for there is none more forbearing than one who submitted himself to slaughter in obedience to his Lord. When He mentioned Ishaq, He called him *alim* (knowing), saying: (Has there come to you the story of the honored guests of Ibrahim? When they entered upon him and said, 'Peace,' he said, 'Peace, a people unknown.') (al-Dhariyat: 24–25), up to His saying: (They said, 'Do not fear,' and gave him good news of a knowing boy) [al-Dhariyat: 28]. This is Ishaq without doubt, because he was from his wife, and she was the one given good news of him, whereas Isma'il was from the concubine. Also, they gave good news of him when Ibrahim was old and had despaired of children, whereas Isma'il was born before that. Also, God the Exalted has established the human custom that the firstborn is more beloved to parents than those after him. When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, asked his Lord for a child and He granted him, a portion of his heart became attached to his love. God the Exalted had taken him as a *khalil* (intimate friend), and intimate friendship is a station that requires the beloved be singled out for love, and that love not be shared with another. When the child took a portion of the father's heart, the jealousy of intimate friendship came to pull it from the heart of the intimate friend, so He commanded him to sacrifice the beloved. When he proceeded to sacrifice him, and the love of God was greater in his heart than the love of the child, the intimate friendship was then purified of the impurities of sharing. There was then no benefit in the slaughter, for the benefit lay in the resolve and in preparing the soul for it, and the purpose had been achieved. So the command was abrogated (*nusikha*), the sacrificed one was ransomed, the intimate friend confirmed the vision, and the Lord's purpose was fulfilled. It is known that this trial and test occurred with the first-born, and would not have occurred with the second-born instead of the first. Indeed, there was not, at the birth of the second child, any competition with the intimate friendship that would require the command to sacrifice him. This is in utmost clarity. Also, Sarah, the wife of the intimate friend, ﷺ, was extremely jealous of Hajar and her son, for she was a slave-girl. When she bore Isma'il and his father loved him, Sarah's jealousy intensified, so God the Exalted commanded that Hajar and her son be sent away from her, and be settled in the land of Makkah, so that the heat of Sarah's jealousy would cool. This was from His mercy and compassion. How then would He command, after this, that he sacrifice her son, and leave the son of the slave-girl as he is? This is with God's mercy toward her, and the removal of harm from her, and His reparation for her. How then would He command, after this, the sacrifice of her son and not the son of the slave-girl? Rather, His perfect wisdom required that He command, after this, the sacrifice of the son of the concubine, so that the lady's heart would soften toward her and her son, and the harshness of jealousy would be transformed into mercy, and the blessing of this slave-girl and her son would be made manifest to her, and that God does not waste a household of which this one and her son are part, and that He show His servants His reparation after breakage, and His kindness after hardship. And that the outcome of the patience of Hajar and her son with separation, solitude, estrangement, and submission to the sacrifice of the child, ended in what it ended in: that their traces and footprints became rites for His believing servants, and acts of worship for them until the Day of Resurrection. This is His way, the Exalted, with whomever He wishes to elevate among His creation: He bestows upon him after weakness, humiliation, and brokenness. God the Exalted said: ﴿And We wished to confer favor upon those who were oppressed in the land and make them leaders and make them the inheritors﴾ [al-Qasas: 5]. That is the bounty of God, which He gives to whom He wills, and God is the possessor of great bounty. See: *al-Isra'iliyyat wa'l-Mawdu'at* by Shaykh Muhammad Abu Shahba, pp. 353–363.]].

It was also said: [the completion of the favor was] by bringing Ya'qub and the tribes (*al-asbat*) out of his loins.

Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: between this dream of Yusuf and its realization, when his parents and brothers came to him, there were forty years. This is the statement of most of the people of *tafsir* (exegesis).

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: between them there were eighty years. When this dream reached the brothers of Yusuf, they envied him and said: "He is not content that his brothers should prostrate to him until his parents prostrate to him as well," so they plotted against him.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Certainly there were in Joseph and his brothers﴾, i.e., in his story and the story of his brothers, ﴿signs﴾. Their names were: Ruwbil (Reuben), who was the eldest of them; Shamʿun (Simeon); Lawi (Levi); Yahudha (Judah); Zabalun (Zebulun), and it was said: Zablun; and Ashir (Asher). Their mother was Liya (Leah), daughter of Layan, and she was the daughter of Yaʿqub's maternal uncle, peace be upon him. And he had four children by his two concubines: the name of one of them was Zilfa and the other Yalhama [in "B": Lamaha], namely Dan, Naftali, and it was said: Naftuli, Jad, and Ashir. Then Liya died, and Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, married her sister Rahil (Rachel), and she bore him Joseph and Binyamin. [And it was said: Wa-bn Yamin] [In "B" this is omitted. Ibn al-Jawzi said in Zad al-Masir (4/183): He was only called Ibn Yamin because his mother died in childbirth, and Yamin means pain.], so the sons of Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, were twelve men.

﴿Signs﴾: Ibn Kathir read "Ayah" in the singular, meaning an admonition and a lesson, and it was said: a wonder.

The others read ﴿Ayat﴾ in the plural.

﴿For those who ask﴾: this is because the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the story of Joseph, peace be upon him.

It was also said: they asked him about the reason the sons of Yaʿqub moved from Canaan to Egypt. He then related to them the story of Joseph, and they found it agreeing with what is in the Torah [so they were amazed by it] [In "B": so they were amazed by him]. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿signs for those who ask﴾ [i.e., evidence of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: signs for those who ask and for those who do not ask, like His saying: ﴿alike for those who ask﴾ (Fussilat 41:10)] [Omitted in "B".].

It was also said: its meaning is a lesson for those who take heed, for it contains the envy of Joseph's brothers and the outcome of their envy; it contains his dream and what Allah fulfilled of it; it contains Joseph's patience against yielding to desire, and his enslavement and imprisonment, and what his affair came to of kingship; it contains Yaʿqub's grief and his patience, and what his affair came to of attaining his desire, and other signs besides these.

﴿When they said: "Joseph and his brother are more beloved to our father than we are"﴾. The *lam* here is the answer to an oath, its implied sense being: "By God, Joseph..." ﴿and his brother﴾ Benjamin ﴿are more beloved to our father than we are﴾. Joseph and his brother Benjamin were from one mother. Ya'qub (peace be upon him) had an exceptionally strong love for Yusuf (peace be upon him), and his brothers saw in his inclination toward him what they did not see in themselves. So they spoke these words. [[Ibn 'Atiyya said (7/440): "Ya'qub's love for Yusuf (peace be upon him) and Benjamin was due to their youth and the death of their mother, and this is the natural human love for the young." It has been related that someone said to the daughter of al-Hasan: "Which of your sons do you love more?" She said: "The young one until he grows up, the absent one until he returns, and the sick one until he recovers."]] ﴿Yet we are a group ('usbah)﴾, a company, and they were ten.

Al-Farra' said: The 'usbah is ten or more.

It was also said: the 'usbah is anything from one to ten.

It was also said: anything from three to ten.

Mujahid said: anything from ten to fifteen.

It was also said: anything from ten to forty.

It was also said: a company whose members support one another, having no singular form from its own root, like *nafar* and *rahT* (men).

﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾, that is, in obvious mistake in preferring Yusuf and his brother over us. The error here does not mean error in religion; had they meant that, they would have disbelieved. Rather, it means error in managing worldly affairs. They were saying: "We are more beneficial to him in worldly matters, in managing his livelihood and tending his livestock, so we deserve his love more than they do. Thus he is mistaken in directing his love toward them."

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verses 9–10:**

﴿Kill Yusuf﴾. The scholars differ over who said these words. Wahb said: it was said by Shim'un (Simeon). Ka'b said: it was said by Dan.

﴿Or cast him out to some land﴾, meaning, to a land far from his father. It was also said: to a land where wild beasts would devour him.

﴿So that your father's attention will be given to you alone﴾, meaning, so that it will be cleared for you and become yours alone.

﴿Your father's face﴾, meaning, so that he will be free from preoccupation with Yusuf. ﴿And after that you will be a righteous people﴾, meaning, after the killing of Yusuf, ﴿righteous﴾, meaning repentant. That is, repent after you have done this, and Allah will forgive you. Muqatil said: your affairs will be set right between you and your father.

﴿One of them said: Do not kill Yusuf﴾. He was Yahudha (Judah). Qatadah said it was Ruwbil (Reuben), who was the son of Yusuf's maternal aunt, and was the eldest of them and the best in his opinion of Yusuf. The first view is more correct, that it was Yahudha, who forbade them from killing him and said: killing is a great and grave sin.

﴿And put him down into the depths of the well﴾. Abu Ja'far and Nafi' recited "ghayabat al-jubb" (in the plural) in both places. The rest recited "ghayabat al-jubb" (in the singular), meaning: at the bottom of the well and in its darkness. Al-ghayabah (the depths) is every place that hides a thing from you and conceals it. Al-jubb is a well that is not lined with stone, because it has been cut (jubb), meaning cut out, and not lined.

﴿Some travellers will pick him up﴾. Al-iltiqat (picking up) is taking a thing from where one does not expect it. ﴿Some of the caravan﴾, meaning some of the travellers, who will take him to another region, so that you will be rid of him. ﴿If you are going to act﴾, meaning, if you are determined to do what you intend. They were, at that time, adults, and they had not yet become prophets.

It was said: they were not adults. This is not correct, as is shown by their saying: ﴿and after that you will be a righteous people﴾.

[Al-Suddi and Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: they intended to restore the condition of their father's heart, and this is likely to have been their intention at that time, and they were not prophets then. The majority said: "righteous" means through repentance, and this is the more evident meaning of the wording, and their situation also indicates it, because they were believers who had committed a great sin and comforted themselves with repentance. See: al-Muharrar al-Wajiz of Ibn 'Atiyyah: 4/443. Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir inclined to the first view, and said in his tafsir (2/470–471): "Know that no proof has been established for the prophethood of Yusuf's brothers, and the apparent context of this passage indicates otherwise. Some people claim that revelation came to them afterwards, but this requires consideration, and whoever claims it needs proof. They have cited nothing except the verse of Allah, the Exalted: (Say: We believe in Allah, and in what has been revealed to us, and in what was revealed to Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the Tribes). This is open to interpretation, because the lineages of the Children of Israel are called the Asbat (tribes), just as the Arabs are called qaba'il (tribes) and the non-Arabs shu'ub (peoples). Allah, the Exalted, mentions that He revealed to prophets from the tribes of the Children of Israel, and He mentioned them collectively because they were many. But each tribe descends from one of the brothers of Yusuf, and no proof has been established that these specific individuals received revelation. And Allah knows best."]

﴿They said: O our father, ask forgiveness for our sins for us﴾. The young one has no sin.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: their action involved grave offences: severing the ties of kinship, disobedience to parents, lack of compassion towards a child who had committed no sin, betrayal of a trust, breaking a covenant, and lying to their father. Allah pardoned them for all of that, so that no one would despair of the mercy of Allah.

Some scholars said: they resolved to kill him, but Allah protected them out of mercy towards them, and had they done it they would all have been destroyed. All of this happened before Allah informed them (of their prophethood).

[This is according to the view that Allah informed them afterwards, which Ibn Kathir described as open to consideration.]

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' was asked: how could they say "we will graze and play" when they were prophets? He said: that was before Allah informed them, and when they agreed to separate him from his father by means of some stratagem.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 11:

﴿They said﴾ to Ya'qub (Jacob), ﴿"O our father, what is [the matter] with you that you do not trust us with Yusuf?"﴾ Abu Ja'far recited: ﴿ta'manna﴾ without ishmam [[In "B": shimma.]], and this is a transmission from Nafi'. The rest recited: ﴿ta'manna﴾ with ishmam of the damma on the first, assimilated nun, and this is an indication toward the damma without pure vocalisation (imhad), so that it is known that its original form was "la ta'manunna" with two nuns, on the pattern of "taf'alu-na," and the first nun was assimilated into the second [[Omitted from "B".]]. They began by objecting to him over his refusal to send him with them, as if they were saying: "You will not send him with us; are you afraid for him from us?"

﴿And indeed we are truly sincere advisers to him﴾. Muqatil said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, because they said to their father: "Send him with us," and their father said: "Indeed, it grieves me that you should take him away," and then they said: ﴿"What is [the matter] with you that you do not trust us with Yusuf? And indeed we are truly sincere advisers to him."﴾ Nusḥ (sincere counsel) here means: attending to his welfare. It was said: it means kindness and tenderness; the meaning is: "We are tender toward him, attending to his welfare, guarding him until we return him to you."

﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ to the desert, ﴿that he may enjoy himself and play﴾. Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿nartaʿ﴾ and ﴿nalʿab﴾ with *nun* in both, and with the *ʿayn* of "nartaʿ" jussive (*jazm*). The people of Kufa read both with *yāʾ* (﴿yartaʿ﴾ and ﴿yalʿab﴾), meaning Yusuf, with the *ʿayn* of "yartaʿ" jussive. Ya'qub read "nartaʿ" with *nun* and "yalʿab" with *yāʾ*.

Al-ratʿ (grazing freely, enjoying abundance) means expansion in pleasures. It is said: "So-and-so ratʿa in his wealth" when he spent it on his desires. The meaning intended is: "and we will indulge ourselves, eat, drink, amuse ourselves and be active."

The people of the Hijaz read ﴿yartaʿ﴾ with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn*, and it is [*yaftaʿil*] [[In "A": *tafʿīl*.]] from *al-raʿy* (pasturing).

Then Ibn Kathir read it with *nun* in both, meaning: "we will guard, and each of us will protect the other."

Abu Ja'far and Nafi' read it with *yāʾ*, reporting about Yusuf, meaning: he pastures the livestock as we pasture them.

﴿Indeed, we will surely guard him﴾.

﴿He [Ya'qub] said﴾ to them: ﴿Indeed, it grieves me that you take him away﴾, meaning: your departure with him grieves me. Here *al-ḥuzn* (grief) is the pain of the heart at separation from the beloved. ﴿And I fear that the wolf may devour him while you are heedless of him﴾. That was because Ya'qub had seen in a dream that a wolf had attacked Yusuf, so he feared for him, and therefore he said this statement. [[Ibn 'Atiyya weakened this view, because if Ya'qub had seen that, it would have been a revelation, and either he would have acted on it, which did not happen, or Ya'qub, through his knowledge of interpreting such visions, would have recognized it and complained about it directly. Unless his saying "I fear that the wolf may devour him" means "I fear that he may suffer what you saw of the wolf's attack," but this is far-fetched. Likewise al-Rabi' ibn Dabi' al-Fazari says: "And I fear the wolf if I pass by it alone, and I fear the wind and the rain." He specified it because it was a creature of common occurrence in the region. It is possible that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, specified it because of Yusuf's young age, meaning: I fear for him from this lowly creature and worse. Likewise al-Rabi' specified it in the previous verse because of its lowliness and weakness among animals. See: al-Muharrar al-Wajiz 4/450-451; al-Bahr al-Muhit 5/286.]]

﴿They said: "If the wolf devours him while we are a band﴾, ten men, ﴿then we would indeed be losers﴾, weak and incapable.

﴿So when they took him away and agreed﴾, meaning resolved, ﴿to put him﴾, meaning to cast him, ﴿into the depths of the well﴾. ﴿And We revealed to him﴾ [[This *waw* is superfluous according to the Kufan grammarians, who hold that it may be added after *lamma* and *ḥattā* and *idhā*, and on that basis they explained the verse ﴿Then when they had both submitted and he had thrown him down upon his forehead, We called out to him﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], meaning: We called out to him. Abu Hayyan said: This view is rejected, because there is nothing in the Qur'an that is superfluous without meaning. The Basran grammarians said: There is no addition in the verse, because the response of *lamma* is omitted, its estimated form being: "When they took him away and agreed to put him in the depths of the well, their trial became great." Some estimated it as: "They put him in it." Abu Hayyan said: This is better, since it is indicated by his saying "and they agreed to put him." See: al-Muharrar al-Wajiz 4/452; al-Bahr al-Muhit 5/287.]], meaning: We revealed to him, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then when they had both submitted…﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], meaning: We called out to him, ﴿that you will surely inform them of this matter of theirs, while they do not perceive﴾. That is: We revealed to Yusuf, peace be upon him, that "you will surely have your dream come true, and you will surely inform your brothers of this deed of theirs while they are unaware of God's revelation and His informing him of that." This is the view of Mujahid.

It was also said: the meaning is: "while they do not perceive" on the day you inform them that you are Yusuf. That was when they entered upon him, and he recognized them while they did not recognize him.

Wahb and others mentioned that they took Yusuf, peace be upon him, with the utmost honor, carrying him, but when they reached the open wilderness they threw him down and began beating him. Whenever one of them struck him, he cried out to another, and the other struck him as well. He found none of them merciful, so they beat him until they nearly killed him, while he shouted: "O my father, if only you knew what the sons of the slave-women are doing to your son!" When they were about to kill him, Yahudha said to them: "Did you not give me a solemn covenant that you would not kill him?" So they took him to the well to throw him into it. He was twelve years old, and it was also said eighteen. They brought him to a well off the road, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top. Muqatil said: it was three farsakhs from the dwelling of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. Ka'b said: between Madyan and Egypt. Wahb said: in the land of Jordan. Qatada said: it was the well of Bayt al-Maqdis. They began lowering him into the well, but he clung to the edge of the well, so they tied his hands and stripped off his shirt. He said: "O brothers, return my shirt to me, so I may cover myself with it in the well." They said: "Call upon the sun, the moon and the stars, and they will keep you company." He said: "I do not see anything," and they cast him into it.

It was also said: they put him in a bucket and sent him down into it until he reached halfway, then they let him fall, intending that he should die. There was water in the well, so he fell into it, then he took refuge on a rock there and stood upon it.

When they cast him into it, he began to weep. They called out to him, and he thought that mercy had reached them, so he answered them. They wanted to crush him with a rock and kill him, but Yahudha prevented them. Yahudha used to bring him food, and he remained in it for three nights. [[Abu Hayyan said concerning such reports from Wahb, Ka'b and others: "The exegetes mentioned many things detailing the manner of his casting into the depths of the well, and his dialogue with them that would soften a rock, while they only grew harder. The Noble Qur'an and the authentic hadith do not address any of them, so they are not to be relied upon in books of tafsir." See: al-Bahr al-Muhit 5/287.]]

﴿And We revealed to him: you will surely inform them of this matter of theirs﴾. Most scholars hold that God, Exalted, revealed this to him and sent Jibril, peace be upon him, to comfort him and give him the good news of deliverance, and to inform him that he would tell them about what they had done and would requite them for it, while they were unaware. [[Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that the revelation to Yusuf at that time came through a messenger, and it is possible that it came by inspiration or sleep, and all of these have been said. Al-Hasan said: God gave him prophethood in the well. This is far-fetched. See: al-Muharrar al-Wajiz 4/453.]]
