Yusuf said: ﴿قُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ الَّذِي فِيهِ تَسْتَفْتِيَانِ﴾ "The matter about which you both inquire has been decided" [[Al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur (4/540) to Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh.]], meaning: the matter about which you ask has been concluded, and Allah's judgment that I told you of has become binding upon you, whether you saw it or did not see it.

﴿وَقَالَ﴾ "And he said," meaning Yusuf at that point, ﴿لِلَّذِي ظَنَّ﴾ "to the one who thought," i.e., knew, ﴿أَنَّهُ نَاجٍ مِنْهُمَا﴾ "that he was going to be saved of the two," and he was the cupbearer, ﴿اذْكُرْنِي عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ﴾ "Mention me to your lord," meaning your master the king, and say to him: "There is a young man in the prison, wrongfully imprisoned, whose confinement has lasted long."

﴿فَأَنْسَاهُ الشَّيْطَانُ ذِكْرَ رَبِّهِ﴾ "But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord." It was said: Satan made the cupbearer forget mentioning Yusuf to the king. Its meaning is: Satan made him forget to mention it to his lord.

Ibn 'Abbas said, and most of the scholars agree: Satan made Yusuf forget the mention of his lord when he sought deliverance from someone other than Allah and sought help from a created being. That was a lapse that came upon Yusuf from Satan [[Abu Hayyan preferred that the pronoun refers to the cupbearer, which is the first opinion, and Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah also preferred it for several reasons. He said: "...Rather, Satan made the one who was saved of the two of them forget the mention of his lord, and this is the correct view, for it agrees with his saying, 'Mention me to your lord.' Allah the Exalted says, 'Satan made him forget the mention of his lord,' and the pronoun returns to the nearest antecedent when there is no evidence to the contrary. Yusuf did not forget the mention of his lord; rather he was constantly mindful of his lord... Then after several points he said: It is clear that His saying 'Satan made him forget the mention of his lord' means: Satan made the youth forget to mention this to his lord, and the one who forgot the mention of Yusuf to his lord... It is clarified that the one who forgot his lord was the youth and not Yusuf by His saying afterward: 'And the one who was saved of the two said, after a while, I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth,' and His saying, 'after a while,' is evidence that he forgot and then remembered." See: Daqa'iq al-Tafsir by Ibn Taymiyyah: 3/259-263, and consult al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan: 5/311-312.]].

﴿فَلَبِثَ﴾ "So he remained," meaning he stayed, ﴿فِي السِّجْنِ بِضْعَ سِنِينَ﴾ "in prison for several years." The scholars differed about the meaning of "bid'" (a few). Mujahid said: between three and seven.

Qatadah said: between three and nine.

Ibn 'Abbas said: fewer than ten.

Most of the commentators hold that "bid'" in this verse means seven years, and he had stayed there five years before that, so the total was twelve years.

Wahb said: Ayyub was afflicted for seven years, Yusuf was left in prison for seven years, and Nebuchadnezzar was punished and transformed among the beasts for seven years [[al-Tabari said in his tafsir (16/115): "The correct view regarding 'bid'' is from three to nine, up to ten, and it cannot be less than three. Likewise, what exceeds the decade up to a hundred, and what exceeds a hundred, cannot be described as 'bid''."]].

Malik ibn Dinar said: When Yusuf said to the cupbearer, "Mention me to your lord," it was said to him: "O Yusuf, you have taken other than Me as a trustee; I will surely prolong your imprisonment." Yusuf wept and said: "O Lord, the multitude of trials has made my heart forget; I spoke a word, and I will not return to it" [[Narrated by al-Tabari in his tafsir: 16/111.]].

Al-Hasan said: Jibril entered upon Yusuf in the prison. When Yusuf saw him, he recognized him and said to him: "O brother of those who warn, why do I see you among the sinners?" Jibril said to him: "O purest of the pure, the Lord of the worlds sends you His greetings and says to you: 'Were you not ashamed before Me, that you sought intercession from human beings? By My might, I will keep you in prison for several years.'" Yusuf said: "And is He pleased with me in that?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then I do not mind."

Ka'b said: Jibril said to Yusuf: "Allah the Exalted says: Who created you?" He said: "Allah." He said: "Who made you beloved to your father?" He said: "Allah." He said: "Who saved you from the distress of the well?" He said: "Allah." He said: "Who taught you the interpretation of dreams?" He said: "Allah." He said: "Who turned away from you evil and immorality?" He said: "Allah." He said: "Then how did you seek intercession from a human being like yourself?" [[These narrations from al-Hasan, Wahb and Malik ibn Dinar are from the Isra'iliyyat (narratives of Israelite origin), and taken together they mean that Yusuf, peace be upon him, remained in prison for several years because of his seeking intercession from the one he knew would be saved, asking him to mention him to his lord. It would have been better for him to rely upon Allah and not say "Mention me to your lord." When he failed to rely upon his Lord, he was requited with a stay in prison for several years. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah refuted this, saying in Daqa'iq al-Tafsir (3/261): "There is nothing in his saying 'Mention me to your lord' that contradicts reliance upon Allah. Indeed, Yusuf himself said, 'Judgment belongs only to Allah,' just as his father's saying, 'Do not enter by one gate, but enter by separate gates,' did not contradict his reliance upon Allah; rather he said, 'I cannot avail you anything against Allah. Judgment belongs only to Allah. Upon Him I rely, and upon Him let those who rely, rely.' Moreover, Allah bore witness that Yusuf was among His sincere servants, and a sincere servant cannot be sincere while relying upon other than Allah, for that is shirk, and Yusuf was not a polytheist, neither in his worship nor in his reliance. He relied upon his Lord regarding his own actions when he said, 'And unless You turn away their plot from me, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant.' So how would he not rely upon Him regarding the actions of His servants? His saying, 'Mention me to your lord,' is like his saying to his Lord, 'Make me over the storehouses of the land; indeed I am a knowing guardian.' When he asked for authority for a religious benefit, that was not a contradiction of reliance, nor was it the forbidden request for leadership. How then would his saying to the youth, 'Mention me...' contradict reliance, when it contains nothing but merely informing the king of him, so that his situation would be known and the truth made clear? Yusuf was among the most steadfast of people. This is why, after the king asked for him ('The king said, bring him to me'), he said: 'Return to your lord and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands? Indeed my Lord is Knowing of their plot.' So Yusuf mentioned his Lord in this situation as he did in that one... There was no abandonment of an obligation in his saying to him, 'Mention me...', nor commission of a forbidden act, for Allah to punish him for it by his remaining in prison for several years. The people had resolved to imprison him for a time before this, unjustly, even though they knew his innocence from the sin, and his remaining in prison was a dignity from Allah in his regard, so that his patience and piety would be completed, for by patience and piety he attained what he attained." When the seven years had passed (al-Kalbi said: these seven were in addition to the five that came before them), and Yusuf's deliverance drew near, the great king of Egypt saw a strange dream that disturbed him. He saw seven fat cows come out of the sea, followed by seven cows, extremely emaciated. The lean ones swallowed the fat ones, and they entered their bellies, and nothing of them was seen, and no trace of them appeared on the lean ones. Then he saw seven green ears of grain whose grain had formed, [and seven others] [[In "b": and seven others.]] dry and ripe for harvest. The dry ones twisted around the green ones until they overpowered them, and nothing of their greenness remained. So he gathered the magicians, the priests, the soothsayers [[In the margin of "a": al-hazzah (ḥāzzah) are the astrologers.]] and the interpreters, and recounted his dream to them. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 43–46:

﴿And the king said: "Indeed, I see seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and others dry."﴾ He said to them: ﴿"O eminent ones, explain to me my vision, if you are able to interpret visions."﴾

﴿They said: "A confusion of dreams."﴾ That is, a mixture of confused dreams, jumbled up things (ahawil). Its singular is dighth (ضِغْث, a bundle), and its origin is a bundle of various kinds of herbage. Al-ahlam (أَحْلَام, dreams) is the plural of al-hulm (الْحُلْم), which is ru'ya (vision). Its verb is halamtu, ahlamu (حَلَمْتُ أَحْلُمُ), with the lam vowelled with fatha in the past tense and with damma in the non-past, ḥuluman and ḥulman, both heavy and light.

﴿"And we are not among those who know the interpretation of dreams."﴾

﴿And the one who was saved﴾ from the killing, ﴿from the two﴾ of the two young men, namely the cupbearer, ﴿and he remembered﴾ i.e. he recalled the words of Yusuf, "Mention me to your lord," ﴿after a period﴾ after a time, which was seven years.

﴿"I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth."﴾ The reason was that the youth knelt before the king and said: "Indeed, there is a man in the prison who interprets visions." ﴿So send me forth﴾ contains an ellipsis; its estimated sense is: "So send me, O king, to him." So he sent him, and he came to the prison. Ibn 'Abbas said: The prison was not in the city.

He said: ﴿"Yusuf, O truthful one (al-siddiq), explain to us regarding seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears and others dry, so that I may return to the people"﴾ of Egypt, ﴿"so that they may know"﴾ the interpretation of the vision. It was also said: "so that they may know your rank in knowledge."

Yusuf said to them, interpreting and teaching: As for the fat cows and the green ears: they are seven years of abundance. And the lean cows and the [dry] ears: they are the barren years of drought. That is the saying of the Exalted about Yusuf, reporting:

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 47–50:

﴿He said: "You will sow for seven years, diligently."﴾ This is a statement with the meaning of a command: that is, "Sow for seven years in your customary manner of cultivation."

Al-da'b (دَأَبًا) means habit or custom. It was also said to mean with earnestness and striving.

ʿĀsim, in the narration of Ḥafs, read ﴿da'aban﴾ with a fatḥah on the hamzah. Both are dialectal forms. It is said: "da'abtu fi al-amr, adba' da'aban and da'ban," meaning I strove diligently in the matter.

﴿And what you reap, leave in its ear, except a little of what you eat.﴾ He commanded them to leave the wheat in its ear so that it would keep longer over time and not spoil, ﴿except a little of what you eat﴾, that is, what you thresh a little of for eating. He commanded them to preserve the greater part and to eat only what is needed.

﴿Then after that will come seven hard years﴾. He called the lean years "hard" because of their severity upon people. ﴿They will consume﴾, that is, they will exhaust and destroy, ﴿what you have stored up for them﴾, that is, the food you have prepared for them will be eaten during them. The eating is attributed to the years by way of figurative extension. ﴿Except a little of what you hoard﴾, that is, what you keep and store aside for seed.

﴿Then after that will come a year in which people will be given rain﴾, that is, they will be sent rain, from al-ghayth, which is rain. It was also said: they will be rescued, from the Arab saying "istaghathtu fulanan fa-aghathani" (I called upon so-and-so for help and he helped me). ﴿And in it they will press﴾. Ḥamzah and al-Kisa'i read "taʿṣirūn" with a tā' because the whole discourse is in the second person, while the others read it with a yā' referring back to "the people." Its meaning: they will press grapes for wine, olives for oil, and sesame for oil. By this he meant abundance of bounty and goodness. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "yaʿṣirūn" means they will be saved from distress and drought; al-ʿaṣar and al-ʿaṣarah mean a place of deliverance and refuge. (Abu ʿUbaydah's statement is in his book Majaz al-Qur'an (1/313–314), and al-Tabari refuted it in his Tafsir (16/131–132), saying: "... This interpretation suffices as evidence of its error: it contradicts the view of all the scholars among the Companions and the Successors.")

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me."﴾ This was because the cupbearer, when he returned to the king and informed him of Yusuf's interpretation of his dream, and the king recognized that what he had said would come to pass, said: "Bring him to me."

﴿So when the messenger came to him﴾ and said to him, "Answer the king," he refused to go out with the messenger until his innocence was made manifest. Then ﴿he said﴾ to the messenger: ﴿"Return to your lord"﴾, meaning your master the king, ﴿and ask him, 'What is the case of the women who cut their hands?'﴾ He did not explicitly mention the wife of al-ʿAzīz, out of courtesy and respect.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Had I remained in prison as long as Yusuf remained, I would have answered the caller." [Narrated by al-Bukhari in the chapter on the Tafsir of Yusuf, "(So when the messenger came to him, he said: Return...)": 8/366.]

﴿Indeed, my Lord is Knower of their plot﴾, that is, indeed Allah is Knowing of their deeds. Yusuf mentioned them only after a long period so that the king would not look upon him with suspicion, and so that he would come to him after doubt about his affair had been removed. Then the messenger returned to the king from Yusuf with his message, and the king summoned the women and the wife of al-ʿAzīz.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "yaʿṣirūn" means they will be saved from distress and drought; al-ʿaṣar and al-ʿaṣarah mean a place of deliverance and refuge. (Abu ʿUbaydah's statement is in his book Majaz al-Qur'an (1/313–314), and al-Tabari refuted it in his Tafsir (16/131–132), saying: "... This interpretation suffices as evidence of its error: it contradicts the view of all the scholars among the Companions and the Successors.")

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me."﴾ This was because the cupbearer, when he returned to the king and informed him of Yusuf's interpretation of his dream, and the king recognized that what he had said would come to pass, said: "Bring him to me."

﴿So when the messenger came to him﴾ and said to him, "Answer the king," he refused to go out with the messenger until his innocence was made manifest. Then ﴿he said﴾ to the messenger: ﴿"Return to your lord"﴾, meaning your master the king, ﴿and ask him, 'What is the case of the women who cut their hands?'﴾ He did not explicitly mention the wife of al-ʿAzīz, out of courtesy and respect.

Yusuf mentioned them only after a long period so that the king would not look upon him with suspicion, and so that he would come to him after doubt about his affair had been removed. Then the messenger returned to the king from Yusuf with his message, and the king summoned the women and the wife of al-ʿAzīz.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 47–50:

﴿He said: "You will sow for seven years, diligently."﴾ This is a statement with the meaning of a command: that is, "Sow for seven years in your customary manner of cultivation."

Al-da'b (دَأَبًا) means habit or custom. It was also said to mean with earnestness and striving.

ʿĀsim, in the narration of Ḥafs, read ﴿da'aban﴾ with a fatḥah on the hamzah. Both are dialectal forms. It is said: "da'abtu fi al-amr, adba' da'aban and da'ban," meaning I strove diligently in the matter.

﴿And what you reap, leave in its ear, except a little of what you eat.﴾ He commanded them to leave the wheat in its ear so that it would keep longer over time and not spoil, ﴿except a little of what you eat﴾, that is, what you thresh a little of for eating. He commanded them to preserve the greater part and to eat only what is needed.

﴿Then after that will come seven hard years﴾. He called the lean years "hard" because of their severity upon people. ﴿They will consume﴾, that is, they will exhaust and destroy, ﴿what you have stored up for them﴾, that is, the food you have prepared for them will be eaten during them. The eating is attributed to the years by way of figurative extension. ﴿Except a little of what you hoard﴾, that is, what you keep and store aside for seed.

﴿Then after that will come a year in which people will be given rain﴾, that is, they will be sent rain, from al-ghayth, which is rain. That is, except those on whom my Lord has mercy and whom He protects. Then he supplicated to him in Hebrew, and the king said: "What is this tongue?" He said: "This is the tongue of my forefathers." The king did not recognize these two tongues.

Wahb said: The king spoke seventy languages. Whenever he spoke in a language, Yusuf answered him in that same language, and he surpassed him by (also speaking) Arabic and Hebrew. So the king was impressed by what he saw of him, despite his young age, for Yusuf was then thirty years old. He seated him, and ﴿said, "Indeed, today you are with us established and trusted."﴾ [Al-Makanah means standing in rank and status.] ﴿Trusted﴾, that is, truthful.

It is also narrated that the king said to him: "I love to hear my dream from you directly."

Yusuf said: "Yes, O king. You saw seven fat cows, white, bright, and beautiful, which the Nile revealed to you. They emerged to you from its bank, their udders dripping milk. While you were looking at them and their beauty pleased you, the Nile suddenly receded, its water diminished, and its dryness appeared. Then seven lean cows, disheveled and dusty, with contracted bellies, came out of its mud—they had no udders or teats—and they had fangs and molars and paws like dogs' paws and snouts like the snouts of beasts. They preyed upon the fat ones like a predator, ate their flesh, tore their skins, crushed their bones, and sucked their marrow. While you were watching and marveling, suddenly seven green ears of grain and seven others dry and black, growing from one root [their roots were in the earth and the water, while you were saying to yourself, 'How can this be? Green and fruitful, and these dry and withered; the source is one, and their roots are in the water'] [[Omitted from "A".]], then a wind blew and scattered the leaves of the dry black ones over the green fruitful ones, and fire ignited among them, and they burned and became black. This is what you saw. Then you awoke from your sleep in fright."

The king said: "By Allah, the matter of this dream, though strange, is not more wondrous than what I have heard from you. So what do you see in my dream, O truthful one?"

Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: "I see that you should gather food and sow a great deal of crops in these fertile years, and store the grain in the granaries with its stalks and ears, so that the stalks and ears may serve as fodder for the animals. The king said: "And who will manage this for me? Who will gather it and sell it, and relieve me of the burden of it?"

Then Yusuf said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land." The treasuries (al-khaza'in) is the plural of khizana, and he meant the storehouses of food and wealth. "The land" means the land of Egypt, i.e., the treasuries of your land.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "Over the revenue (kharaj) of Egypt and its income."

"Indeed, I am a guardian, knowing." That is: a guardian of the treasuries, knowing the ways of their proper management. It was also said: "a guardian, knowing." It was also said: a guardian of what you entrust to me, knowing what you appoint me to.

It was also said: a guardian for the reckoning, knowing the languages, I know the language of everyone who comes to me.

Al-Kalbi said: "A guardian of its measure during the years of plenty (in the barren land), knowing the time of hunger when it occurs." So the king said to him, "And who is more deserving of it than you?!" So he appointed him to that and said to him, "Indeed, today you are with us firmly established, of high rank and standing, trustworthy over the treasuries."

Abu Sa'id al-Shurayhi informed us, Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi informed us, Abu 'Abdullah al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Fanjawi informed me, Makhlad ibn Ja'far al-Baqarji narrated to us, al-Hasan ibn 'Alawayh narrated to us, Isma'il ibn 'Isa narrated to us, Ishaq ibn Bishr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Yusuf. Had he not said, 'Appoint me over the treasuries of the land,' he would have employed him at once. But he delayed it for a year, so he remained in his house for a year with the king." [[A fabricated (mawdu') hadith. The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in "al-Kafi al-Shaf" p. (90): "al-Tha'labi narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas through the transmission of Ishaq ibn Bishr, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from him. This chain is wholly unsound." Al-Albani said: "It was also narrated through al-Tha'labi by al-Wahidi in his tafsir." (Silsilat al-Ahadith al-Da'ifah) (1/335).]]

And with its chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: When the year had passed from the day on which he asked for the governorship, the king summoned him. He was adorned [and girded with his sword] [[In "b": "and draped him with his sword."]] and placed for him a throne of gold set with pearls and rubies, and spread over it a silk brocade (istabraq). The length of the throne was thirty cubits and its width ten cubits. On it were thirty cushions and sixty coverings. Then he ordered him to go out, and he went out crowned. His complexion was like snow and his face like the moon; the beholder could see his face reflected in the clarity of its color. He proceeded until he sat upon the throne, and kings submitted to him. The king entered his house and entrusted to him the affairs of Egypt, removed Qitfir from what he had held, and made Yusuf in his place, as related by Ibn Ishaq. [[Ibn 'Atiyyah cited this report from Ibn Ishaq, then said: "Similar narratives of this kind have been related which cannot be verified for authenticity, and their full recitation would be lengthy." See: al-Muharrar al-Wajiz (8/8).]]

Ibn Zayd said: The king of Egypt had many treasuries, so he handed over all his authority to him, and made his command and judgment binding. They said: Then Qitfir died during those nights, and the king married Yusuf to Ra'il, the wife of Qitfir. When he entered upon her, he said, "Is this not better than what you used to desire?" She said, "O truthful one, do not blame me, for I was a beautiful, pampered woman, as you see, in rule and worldly comfort, and my husband did not approach women, and you were as Allah made you in beauty and bearing, so my self overpowered me." Yusuf found her a virgin and had intercourse with her, and she bore him two sons: Ephraim (Afrathim) son of Yusuf, and Manasseh (Misha) son of Yusuf. [[Ibn 'Atiyyah cited this report from Ibn Ishaq, then said: "Similar narratives of this kind have been related which cannot be verified for authenticity, and their full recitation would be lengthy." See: al-Muharrar al-Wajiz (8/8).]]

The rule of Egypt became firmly established for Yusuf, i.e., it was consolidated. He established justice among them, and both men and women loved him. This is the meaning of the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 56–57:

﴿And thus did We establish Joseph in the land﴾, meaning: the land of Egypt; We made him its king [[In manuscript "A": makkannah.]], ﴿to settle therein wherever he willed﴾, that is: to dwell where he pleased and to do therein whatever he willed.

Ibn Kathir read "nashaʾu" (we will) with the nun, in response to His saying ﴿makkanna﴾ ("We established"), while the others read it with the ya' (yaʾ, "he will"), in response to His saying ﴿yatabawwaʾu﴾ ("he settles").

﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾, that is: with Our blessing, ﴿and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Wahb said: this means those who are patient.

Mujahid and others said: Joseph, peace be upon him, continued to invite the king to Islam and to gently persuade him until the king and many of the people embraced Islam. This is in this world.

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter﴾ is the reward of the Hereafter, ﴿is better for those who believed and used to be God-fearing﴾.

They were people of the desert, with camels and sheep. Ya'qub (peace be upon him) summoned them and said: "O my sons, I have heard that in Egypt there is a righteous king who sells food. So prepare yourselves and go to buy food from him." He sent them, and they came to Egypt. ﴿Then they entered upon him﴾, that is, upon Yusuf. ﴿And he recognized them﴾, Yusuf (peace be upon him).

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: he recognized them the moment he first looked at them.

Al-Hasan said: he did not recognize them until they made themselves known to him.

﴿While they did not recognize him﴾, that is, they did not recognize him. Ibn 'Abbas said: between the time they threw him into the well and the time they entered upon him there were forty years, and therefore they did not recognize him.

'Ata' said: they did not recognize him because he was on the throne of kingship, with the crown of kingship on his head.

It was also said: because he was dressed in the manner of the kings of Egypt, wearing garments of silk and with a collar of gold around his neck. When Yusuf looked at them, and they spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them: "Tell me who you are and what your matter is, for I find your situation strange." They said: "We are a people from the land of the Levant, herdsmen. Hardship has befallen us, so we have come seeking grain."

He said: "Perhaps you have come to spy out the weak points of my land."

They said: "No, by God, we are not spies. We are brothers, sons of one father, and he is an elderly, truthful man called Ya'qub [[In "A": siddiq.]], a prophet of the prophets of God."

He said: "And how many are you?" They said: "We were twelve. One of our brothers went out with us into the desert and perished there, and he was the most beloved of us to our father."

He said: "And how many are you here?"

They said: "Ten."

He said: "And where is the other?"

They said: "With our father, for he is the full brother of the one who perished, and our father finds consolation in him."

He said: "Who will confirm that what you say is true?"

They said: "O king, we are in a land where none of its people knows us [from among its inhabitants] [[Omitted from "B".]]."

Then Yusuf said: "Bring me your brother who is your father's son, if you are truthful, and I will be satisfied with that."

They said: "Our father grieves over his separation from him, and we will try to persuade his father."

He said: "Leave one of you with me as a pledge until you bring me your brother." So they cast lots among themselves, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, and he was the most judicious of them concerning Yusuf, so they left him with him. This is the meaning of His words, mighty and majestic is He:

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 59–62:

﴿When he had equipped them with their provisions﴾, that is, he loaded a camel for each one of them with their supplies, ﴿he said: "Bring me a brother of yours from your father"﴾, meaning Benjamin, ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?﴾ That is, I complete the measure and do not shortchange people in anything, so I will add a camel's load for the sake of your brother, honour your station, and treat you well. ﴿And I am the best of those who host﴾. Mujahid said: that is, the best of hosts. He had treated them with excellent hospitality.

﴿But if you do not bring him to me, then there will be no measure for you with me﴾, that is, you will have no food from me to measure out for yourselves, ﴿and do not come near me﴾, that is, do not come near my house or my land after that. This is a jussive (jazm) in the sense of a prohibition.

﴿They said: "We will seek to persuade our father about him"﴾, that is, we will request him and ask him to send him with us, ﴿and we will certainly do it﴾, what you have commanded us.

﴿And he said to his servants﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿lifityanihi﴾ with an alif and a nun, while the rest read "liftayatihi" with a ta' and without an alif, meaning "to his boys". Both are dialectal forms, like al-sibyan and al-sibyah. ﴿"Put their merchandise"﴾, that is, the price of their food, and it was in dirhams.

Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas: it was sandals and leather.

It was also said: it was eight skins of ground-meal (suwiq al-muql). The first view is more sound.

﴿in their saddlebags﴾, that is, their containers, and it is the plural of rahl, ﴿so that they may recognize it when they return to their family, so that they may come back﴾, that is, when they have gone back.

The scholars differed about the reason Joseph did this. It was said: he wished to show them his generosity in returning the merchandise and in placing the guarantee in kindness and benevolence, so that it would be more inviting for them to return. "So that they may recognize it" means: his honour toward them.

It was also said: he saw it as baseness to take the price of food from his father and brothers while they were in need of it, so he returned it to them, without their knowing, out of generosity.

Al-Kalbi said: he feared that his father would not have enough silver with which they could return a second time.

It was also said: he did this because he knew that their religious faith would drive them to return the merchandise, to rule out error, and that they would not consider it lawful to keep it.

﴿And He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾

When they opened their belongings, [the goods] they had carried from Egypt, they found their merchandise (bidā'atahum), the price of the food, had been returned to them. They said: "O our father, what more could we desire?" That is: what else do we seek, what more could we want? The reason is that they had told Ya'qub (peace be upon him) of the king's kindness toward them, and urged him to send Binyamin with them. So when they opened the goods and found the merchandise, they said: "This is our merchandise, returned to us." That is, what more could we ask for by way of speech? This is the plain evidence of kindness and generosity: he has given us full measure and returned our price to us. They intended to comfort their father's heart. "And we will bring provisions for our family": that is, we will buy food for them and carry it back to them. It is said: māra ahlahu yamīru mayran, when he brought food to his family from one town [to another town] [[omitted in "B".]]. Its equivalent is imtāra yamtāru imtiyāran.

"And we will guard our brother" Binyamin, that is, from whatever you fear for him.

"And we will gain" an extra load on our camels, "a camel's load" – that is, a camel's load of measure will be measured out for us because of him, for he (the king) used to give a camel's load in the name of each man. "That is an easy measure" [That is: what we have carried is little, and will not suffice us and our family. It is also said: the meaning is that we will gain a camel's load; that is an easy measure] [[omitted in "B".]], involving no burden and no hardship.

Mujahid said: "The camel here is the donkey. A camel's load means a donkey's load, and this is a dialect; a donkey is called ba'ir." They were people who owned donkeys. The first view is more sound, that it is the well-known camel.

He [Ya'qub] said to them: "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn covenant (mawthiqan) from God," – a pledge and an oath – "and the covenant made firm (al-mawthiq) is the one confirmed by an oath. It is also said: it is the one confirmed [by calling God to witness] [[in "B": by the testimony.]] against oneself – "that you will surely bring him back to me." He introduced the lam into the statement because the meaning of the words is an oath. "Unless you are encompassed (yuhāṭa bikum)." Mujahid said: "Unless you are all destroyed."

Qatadah said: "Unless you are overpowered so that you cannot do it."

It is related in the story that the brothers were pressed by the matter and exerted themselves to the utmost, so Ya'qub had no choice but to send Binyamin with them.

It is also said: a guardian. Ka'b said: When Ya'qub said, "God is the best guardian," God, Mighty and Majestic, said: "By My might, I will surely return both of them to you after you have put your trust in Me."

When they opened their belongings, [the goods] they had carried from Egypt, they found their merchandise (bidā'atahum), the price of the food, had been returned to them. They said: "O our father, what more could we desire?" That is: what else do we seek, what more could we want? The reason is that they had told Ya'qub (peace be upon him) of the king's kindness toward them, and urged him to send Binyamin with them. So when they opened the goods and found the merchandise, they said: "This is our merchandise, returned to us." That is, what more could we ask for by way of speech? This is the plain evidence of kindness and generosity: he has given us full measure and returned our price to us. They intended to comfort their father's heart. "And we will bring provisions for our family": that is, we will buy food for them and carry it back to them. It is said: māra ahlahu yamīru mayran, when he brought food to his family from one town [to another town] [[omitted in "B".]]. Its equivalent is imtāra yamtāru imtiyāran.

"And we will guard our brother" Binyamin, that is, from whatever you fear for him.

"And we will gain" an extra load on our camels, "a camel's load" – that is, a camel's load of measure will be measured out for us because of him, for he (the king) used to give a camel's load in the name of each man. **Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verses 73–76:**

﴿They said﴾, meaning the brothers of Yusuf, ﴿By God﴾, that is, "by Allah." This expression is singled out for the replacement of the *waw* with a *ta'* in oaths, unlike the other names of Allah, the Exalted.

﴿You know well that we did not come to cause corruption in the land﴾, meaning, that we would not steal in the land of Egypt.

If it is asked: How did they say "you know well," and from where did they know this?

It is answered: They said "you know well that we did not come to cause corruption in the land," for since we took this route we have not harmed anyone, so ask about us those whom we have passed by: Have we harmed anyone?

It is also said: It is because they returned the merchandise that had been placed in their saddlebags. They said: "If we were thieves, we would not have returned it."

It is also said: They said that because they were known for not taking what was not theirs. And whenever they entered Egypt, they would muzzle the mouths of their animals so that they would not eat any of the people's crops.

﴿And we were not thieves﴾.

﴿They said﴾, meaning the herald and his companions: ﴿Then what is the penalty for it﴾, that is, the penalty for the thief, ﴿if you are liars﴾ in your statement "we were not thieves."

﴿They said﴾ [meaning: the brothers of Yusuf] [[Addition from "b".]], ﴿The penalty for it is: whoever is found in his saddlebag, he himself is its penalty﴾, that is: the penalty for the thief is that the thief be handed over, because of his theft, to the one from whom he stole, so that he is enslaved for a year. This was the established practice (sunnah) of the family of Ya'qub regarding the judgment on a thief. The ruling of the king of Egypt, however, was that the thief be beaten and made to pay twice the value of the stolen goods. Yusuf wished to detain his brother with him, so he referred the judgment to them, in order to be able to keep him with him according to their ruling.

﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, those who commit what is not lawful for them to do, namely stealing the property of others.

At that point the messenger said: "There is no alternative but to search your belongings."

So he began searching them. It is narrated that he brought them back to Yusuf, and he ordered that their containers be searched in his presence.

﴿So he began with their containers﴾, to remove suspicion, ﴿before the container of his brother﴾. So he would search their containers one by one. Qatadah said: We were told that he would not open a bundle nor look into a container without seeking forgiveness from Allah, out of remorse for the accusation he had made against them, until only the saddlebag of Binyamin remained. He said: "I do not think this one took it." His brothers said: "By Allah, we will not leave until you search his saddlebag, for that will be better for your soul and for ours." When they opened his bundle, they took it out from it. This is the meaning of His, the Exalted's, words:

﴿Then he brought it out from his brother's container﴾. The pronoun in His words "then he brought it out" is feminine, although *al-sawā'* (the cup) is masculine, as shown by His words "and for whoever brings it, a camel's load." The reason is that here the pronoun refers back to the *siqayah* (the drinking vessel).

It is also said: *al-sawā'* may be treated as both masculine and feminine. When the cup was brought out from Binyamin's saddlebag, his brothers lowered their heads in shame, turned to Binyamin and said: "What have you done? You have disgraced us and blackened our faces, O son of Rahil! Your troubles never cease for us. When did you take this cup?" Binyamin said: "Rather, the sons of Rahil never cease to have troubles from you. You took my brother and destroyed him in the wilderness. And this one [Yusuf] placed the cup in my saddlebag, just as he placed the merchandise in your saddlebags." So they seized Binyamin as a slave [[See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/200; Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/355.]].

It is also said: that man seized him by the neck and brought him back to Yusuf, as thieves are brought back.

﴿Thus We devised for Yusuf﴾. The *kayd* (scheme) here is a recompense for a scheme: that is, just as they had devised against Yusuf at the beginning, We devised in return. Ya'qub, peace be upon him, had said to Yusuf: "lest they scheme against you a scheme," so We devised for Yusuf in regard to their matter.

*Al-kayd* from creatures is cunning (ḥīlah), and from Allah, the Exalted, it is planning in accordance with truth. It is also said: *kidna* means "We inspired"; it is also said: "We arranged"; it is also said: "We willed." Its meaning: We contrived for Yusuf until he drew his brother to himself and kept him away from his brothers.

﴿He could not have taken his brother﴾, so as to keep him with himself, ﴿under the king's law﴾, that is, under his judgment. Qatadah said this. Ibn Abbas said: "under his authority."

﴿Unless Allah wills﴾. That is: Yusuf would not have been able to detain his brother under the king's judgment, had it not been for what We devised for him through Our kindness, until he found the way to that, namely what He caused to flow on the tongues of the brothers, that the penalty for a thief is enslavement. Thus Yusuf's aim was achieved by the will of Allah, the Exalted.

﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ through knowledge, just as We raised Yusuf's rank above his brothers. Ya'qub recited *yarfa'u* and *yashā'u* with the *ya'* in both. [The attachment of *darajāt* to *man* in this surah: the correct view is that the verb in both is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, and His mention has already preceded in His words: "unless Allah wills," meaning: Allah raises the degrees of whom He wills. The rest recited with the *nun* in both, except that the Kufans recited *darajātin* with tanwin, while others read it with the construct (iḍāfah), meaning: "We raise by means of him," and the one who raises is also Allah, the Exalted.] [[What is between the brackets is omitted from "b".]]

﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾. Ibn Abbas said: Above every scholar is a scholar, until knowledge ends with Allah, the Exalted. So Allah, the Exalted, is above every scholar.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: his maternal grandfather had an idol that he worshipped, so Yusuf took it secretly, or broke it and threw it in the road so that it would not be worshipped.[[Narrated by Ibn Jarir in his Tafsir: 16/195. See also al-Durr al-Manthur: 4/564.]]

Mujahid said: once a beggar came to Yusuf, so he took an egg from the house and gave it to the beggar. Sufyan ibn Uyaynah said: he took a hen from the birds that were in the house of Ya'qub and gave it to a beggar. Wahb said: he would set aside food from the table for the poor.[[See al-Durr al-Manthur: 4/564.]]

Muhammad ibn Ishaq mentioned that Yusuf was with his paternal aunt, the daughter of Ishaq, after the death of his mother Rahil. His aunt nursed him and loved him intensely. When he grew up, Ya'qub's love for him became strong, so he came to her and said: "O sister, hand Yusuf over to me, for by Allah I cannot bear that he be out of my sight for an hour." She said: "No, by Allah." He said: "By Allah, I will not leave him." She said: "Leave him with me for a few days, so that I may look at him; perhaps that will console me about him." He did so. She then took a girdle (mintaqah) of Ishaq, which they had inherited through seniority, for it was with her because she was the eldest child of Ishaq. She fastened the girdle under Yusuf's clothes while he was small, then said: "I have lost the girdle of Ishaq. Search the household!" They searched and found it with Yusuf. She said: "By Allah, he is my captive (salam li)." Ya'qub said: "If he did that, then he is your captive (salam laka)."[[al-Salam (with two fathahs): the submission of one who yields and is abased, like a prisoner who does not resist the one who commands him. One says "akhadhahu salaman" when he has taken him captive without a battle, so he comes along submissive and does not resist. See the edition of Mahmud Shakir of al-Tabari: 16/196.]] She then kept him with her until she died. This is what the brothers of Yusuf meant: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has indeed stolen before.﴾[[Narrated by al-Tabari: 16/196-197, and al-Suyuti attributed it to Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim. (al-Durr al-Manthur: 4/563). However, no authentic text from the Prophet ﷺ has been transmitted specifying the theft with which they charged him, and Allah knows best what occurred.]]

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verses 78–79:**

﴿They said: "O Chief, indeed he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good."﴾ It is related in the story that they became exceedingly angry at this situation. The sons of Ya'qub (Jacob), when they became angry, could not be restrained, and Ruwbil (Reuben), when he became angry, nothing could withstand his anger. When he shouted, every pregnant woman who heard his voice would miscarry her child. Yet, despite this, if any of the sons of Ya'qub touched him, his anger would subside.

It is also said that this was the characteristic of Shim'un (Simeon), one of the sons of Ya'qub.

It is narrated that he said to his brothers: "How many markets are there in Egypt?" They said, "Ten." He said: "You take care of the markets, and I will take care of the king; or you take care of the king, and I will take care of the markets." So they entered upon Yusuf (Joseph), and Ruwbil said: "Either you return our brother to us, or I will let out a cry that will leave no pregnant woman in Egypt without miscarrying her child." Every hair on Ruwbil's body stood up and burst out of his garments. Then Yusuf said to a young son of his: "Stand beside Ruwbil and touch him." It is also reported: "Take hold of his hand and bring him to me." So the boy went and touched him, and his anger subsided. Then Ruwbil said: "Indeed, here is a scion (bizr, meaning offspring; it is said, 'How abundant is his bizr!' meaning his children) of Ya'qub." Yusuf said: "Who is Ya'qub?"

It is also related that he became angry a second time, so Yusuf rose toward him, kicked him with his foot, and seized him by the collar, so that he fell to the ground. Yusuf said: "You, the company of the Hebrews (al-'Ibraniyyin), do you think that no one is stronger than you?"

When their affair had reached this point, and they saw that there was no way for them to free him, they submitted and humbled themselves, and said: "O Chief, indeed he has an aged father who loves him, so take one of us in his place, (﴿فَخُذْ أَحَدَنَا مَكَانَهُ﴾) instead of him, (﴿إِنَّا نَرَاكَ مِنَ الْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾) indeed we see you as one of the doers of good in your conduct."[[Related by al-Tabari at length in his Tarikh (1/355–356), and in abridged form in his Tafsir (16/200–201).]] It is also said: "one of the doers of good toward us in giving full measure, in good hospitality, and in returning the merchandise." And it is said: they meant, "If you do this, you will be among the doers of good."

﴿He said﴾: Yusuf said, ﴿"I seek refuge in Allah"﴾: I take refuge in Allah, ﴿"from taking anyone except him with whom we found our property"﴾. He did not say "except the one who stole," out of caution against lying. ﴿"Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers"﴾: if we took an innocent person in place of a guilty one.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (*Ma'alim al-Tanzil*) on surah 12, verse 80:

﴿فَلَمَّا اسْتَيْئَسُوا مِنْهُ﴾ *So when they despaired of him*, meaning they despaired that Yusuf would grant them what they had asked. Abu 'Ubayda said: *istay'asu* means they became certain that the brother would not be returned to them.

﴿خَلَصُوا نَجِيًّا﴾ *They withdrew to confer privately*, meaning some of them went off alone with one another, conferring and consulting, with no one else mixing with them.

*Najiyy* can apply to a group, as here, and it can apply to a single person, as in His saying: ﴿وَقَرَّبْنَاهُ نَجِيًّا﴾ *And We brought him near as a confidant* [Maryam: 52]. It may be used for both one and many because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) used as an adjective, like *'adl* (justice) and *zawr* (falsehood). Similarly, *najwa* can be a noun or a verbal noun. God Most High said: ﴿وَإِذْ هُمْ نَجْوَى﴾ *when they were confidants* [al-Isra': 47], meaning "conferring privately." He said: ﴿مَا يَكُونُ مِنْ نَجْوَى ثَلَاثَةٍ﴾ *There is no private conference among three* [al-Mujadila: 7], and He said of the verbal noun: ﴿إِنَّمَا النَّجْوَى مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ﴾ *Private conferring is only from Satan* [al-Mujadila: 10].

﴿قَالَ كَبِيرُهُمْ﴾ *Their eldest said*: meaning in intellect and knowledge, not in age. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi said: he is Yahudha, and he was the most intelligent of them. Mujahid said: he is Sham'un, and leadership over his brothers belonged to him. Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: he is Ruben, who was the oldest of them in age, and he is the one who forbade the brothers from killing Yusuf. [[The narrations mentioned here are cited by al-Suyuti in *al-Durr al-Manthur*: 4/565, and by al-Tabari in his *Tafsir*: 16/206–208. Al-Tabari, favouring "Ruben," said: "The most correct of the views on this is the view of those who said that by His saying 'their eldest' is meant Ruben, because all of them agree that he was the oldest of them in age. When the Arabs are addressed with 'so-and-so is the eldest of the people' without any qualification, they understand only one of two meanings: either leadership and lordship over them, or age. As for intellect, if they intend that they say 'he is the eldest of them in intellect.' When it is stated without such a qualifier, only what I have mentioned is understood. The people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) have said: Sham'un did not have leadership and lordship over his brothers, although he had the standing in knowledge and intellect that God granted him, so it is known that by His saying 'their eldest' He meant the other sense, which is age. Since this is so, only the remaining sense is left, which is seniority in age. And all those we mentioned have said: 'Ruben was the oldest of them in age,' so the view we have chosen is confirmed."]]

﴿أَلَمْ تَعْلَمُوا أَنَّ أَبَاكُمْ قَدْ أَخَذَ عَلَيْكُمْ مَوْثِقًا﴾ *Did you not know that your father had taken a covenant from you*, meaning a pledge.

﴿مِنَ اللَّهِ وَمِنْ قَبْلُ مَا فَرَّطْتُمْ﴾ *from God, and before this you failed*, meaning you were negligent (*qassartum*) ﴿فِي يُوسُفَ﴾ *concerning Yusuf*. The scholars differed over the grammatical position of *ma*. It was said that it is in the accusative case, governed by the verb of knowledge, meaning: "Did you not know, before your neglect concerning Yusuf?" [And it was said that it is in the nominative case as the subject (*mubtada'*), and the sentence is complete at His saying ﴿مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾, then He said ﴿وَمِنْ قَبْلُ﴾, meaning: "this is your neglect concerning Yusuf."] [The text within the brackets is absent from manuscript "B."] It was also said that *ma* is an extra particle (*sila*), meaning: "And before this you failed concerning Yusuf."

﴿فَلَنْ أَبْرَحَ الْأَرْضَ﴾ *So I will not leave the land*, namely the land in which I am, which is the land of Egypt, ﴿حَتَّى يَأْذَنَ لِي أَبِي﴾ *until my father gives me permission*, to leave it and calls me back, ﴿أَوْ يَحْكُمَ اللَّهُ لِي﴾ *or God decides for me*, by returning my brother to me, or by my departure and leaving my brother behind. It was also said: or God decides for me by the sword, so that I fight them and recover my brother.

﴿وَهُوَ خَيْرُ الْحَاكِمِينَ﴾ *And He is the best of judges*, meaning the most just of those who decide between people.

﴿Return to your father﴾. The brother who was detained [in Egypt] [[Omitted from manuscript "A".]] says to his brothers: return to your father, ﴿and say, "O our father, indeed your son"﴾, Benjamin, ﴿has stolen﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḍaḥḥak recited "suriqa" with a dammah on the sīn, a kasrah on the rāʾ, and a shaddah, meaning: he was attributed to theft, just as one says "khawwantuhu," meaning I attributed to him betrayal.

﴿And we bear witness only to what we know﴾ [meaning: we said this only on the basis of what we knew], [[Omitted from manuscript "B".]] for we saw the drinking cup taken out of his belongings. It was also said that the meaning is: "And we did not bear witness," that is, we never gave testimony about anything during our lifetime except on the basis of what we knew, and this is not a testimony from us; it is merely a report about the conduct of your son according to their claim.

It was also said: Jacob, peace be upon him, said to them: "This man does not know that a thief is taken for his theft except by your saying," and they replied: "We did not testify before Joseph that a thief is enslaved except on the basis of what we knew." And that was the ruling among the prophets, Jacob and his sons.

﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾. Mujāhid and Qatādah said: We did not know that your son would steal and that our affair would come to this; had we known that, we would not have gone with him. We only said "and we will guard our brother" from what we had no means of guarding him against. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: we were not guardians of his night and his day, nor of his coming and going. ʿIkrimah said: "And we were not guardians of the unseen" means that perhaps it was secretly placed in his baggage at night.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 82–84:

﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾ — i.e., the people of the town, and it is Egypt. Ibn ʿAbbas said: It is a town from the towns of Egypt; they had set out from it toward Egypt.

﴿And the caravan in which we came back﴾ — i.e., the caravan in which we were. With them were some people from Canaan, neighbours of Yaʿqub. Ibn Ishaq said: The brother who was detained in Egypt knew that his brothers were under suspicion in the eyes of their father because of what they had done in the matter of Yusuf, so he instructed them to say this to their father.

﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾. If it is said: How could Yusuf permit himself to do such a thing to his father, not informing him of his whereabouts, and detaining his brother while knowing how intense his father's grief over him was, and there is in this a meaning of disobedience, severing of kinship and little compassion? It is said: People have said much on this, and the correct view is that he did that by the command of Allah, the Exalted, Who commanded him to do so, in order to increase the trial of Yaʿqub, so that He might multiply his reward and raise him in rank to his forefathers who had passed. It is also said: He did not reveal himself to his brothers because he did not feel safe that they would plot against him and conceal him from their father. The first view is more sound.

﴿He said: Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you﴾ — "zayyanat" (made attractive). There is an ellipsis in it; its meaning is: They returned to their father and related to him what their eldest had said, and Yaʿqub said: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you﴾, i.e., your brother was taken to Egypt in pursuit of an immediate benefit.

﴿So patience is fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾ — meaning: Yusuf, Binyamin, and their brother who remained in Egypt.

﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing﴾ — of my sorrow and my grief over their loss, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ — in the management of His creation.

The saying of the Most High: ﴿And he turned away from them﴾. That is because when the news of Binyamin reached Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, his sorrow was complete and his distress reached its height, and his grief over Yusuf was stirred up, so he turned away from them. ﴿And he said: Alas for Yusuf!﴾ — i.e., "Alas, my sorrow!" ﴿And his eyes turned white from grief﴾ — his sight became blind. Muqatil said: He did not see with them for six years. ﴿So he was suppressing [his grief]﴾ — i.e., full of grief, restraining it, not disclosing it. Qatadah said: He kept his grief within his chest and said nothing but good. Al-Hasan said: Between Yusuf's departure from his father's lap and the day he met him there were eighty years; Yaʿqub's eyes never dried, and on the face of the earth on that day there was no one more honoured by Allah than Yaʿqub.

**[Commentary of al-Baghawi, *Ma'alim al-Tanzil*, on Surah 12, verses 85–86]**

﴿They said﴾ meaning: the sons of Ya'qub, ﴿By Allah, you will not cease remembering Yusuf﴾, that is: you will not stop remembering Yusuf, you will not slacken in your love for him. The "not" (*la*) is omitted from the phrase ﴿taftaʾu﴾. It is said: *ma fati'a yafʿalu kadha*, meaning *ma zala* (he did not cease doing such-and-such), as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"I said: By Allah's oath, I will not leave standing, even if they cut off my head and my limbs before you."* [[The verse is in the Diwan of Imru' al-Qays, p. 32. al-Tabari cites it in 4/425 and 16/221, and Ibn Qutaybah in al-Mushkil, p. 174, where the word "qa'idan" (sitting) appears instead of "qa'iman" (standing).]]

That is: *la abrah* (I will not leave).

﴿Until you become a *haradan*﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: *dafan* (close to death, i.e. sick and wasted). Mujahid said: *al-haradu* is what falls short of death, meaning close to death. Ibn Ishaq said: corrupt, without reason.

*Al-haradu* is one whose body and mind have deteriorated. It is also said: melting away from grief. The meaning of the verse is: until you become one whose body is worn out and whose mind is deranged.

The root of *haradu* is corruption of body and mind from sorrow, old age, or love (*'ishq*). From this is the saying of al-'Arji: [[The verse is quoted by Ibn Ishaq's line; the sense is: "I am a man whom love has seized, and it has wasted me (*ahradani*), until I was worn out, and illness has made me thin."]] *"I am a man whom love has seized, so it has made me a haradu, until I was worn out, and affliction has emaciated me."* He means by "*fa-ahradani*": it melted me and left me a *muhrad* (one reduced to a wreck).

It is said: *rajulun haradun* (a man who is a haradu), *imra'atun haradun* (a woman who is a haradu), *rajulani wa-imra'atani haradun* (two men or two women who are a haradu), and *rijalun wa-nisa'un kadhalika* (men and women likewise). The singular, dual, plural, masculine and feminine are all alike in this, because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) placed in the position of a noun. [[When this word is used as a descriptive adjective, it takes the dual and plural forms and the masculine and feminine forms. But "haradu" is always kept in the singular form and never takes the feminine marker, because it is a verbal noun. If it is formed as a *fa'il* pattern, in the manner of nouns, it takes on what nouns take: dual, plural, masculine and feminine. See al-Tabari 16/222.]]

﴿Or you become among those who perish﴾, that is: among the dead.

﴿He said﴾: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, at that moment, when he saw their harshness: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾. *Al-batthu* is the most intense grief. It is named so because the one who has it cannot bear it until he *yuthbitahu*, that is, reveals it. Al-Hasan said: *bathhi* means my need.

It is reported that a neighbour of his came to Ya'qub and said: "O Ya'qub, why do I see you broken and worn out? You have not reached the age that your father reached." He said: "What has broken me and worn me down is the trial Allah has afflicted me with, the grief over Yusuf." Allah revealed to him: "O Ya'qub, do you complain to My creatures?" He said: "O Lord, it was a sin I committed, so forgive it for me." He said: "I have forgiven it for you." After that, whenever he was asked, he would say: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾. [[Reported by al-Tabari in his Tafsir 16/227–228 from Talhah ibn Musarrif al-Yami, as a statement of his (mawquf). In the original it is "al-Iyami," and the form "al-Yami" is taken from Tahdhib al-Tahdhib, where he is described as a Kufan, learned reciter, of the fifth generation.]]

It is also reported that he was asked: "O Ya'qub, what took away your sight and bent your back?" He said: "My weeping for Yusuf took away my sight, and my grief for his brother bent my back." So Allah revealed to him: "Do you complain about Me? By My might and My majesty, I will not remove what is upon you until you call upon Me."

At that point he said: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾. Then Allah revealed to him: "By My might and My majesty, if they were both dead I would have brought them out for you. But I was displeased with you because you slaughtered a sheep, and a poor man stood at your door, and you did not give him any of it. The dearest of My creatures to Me are the prophets, then the poor. So prepare food and invite the poor to it."

So he prepared food and then said: "Whoever is fasting, let him break his fast tonight at the household of Ya'qub." [[Reported by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak from Anas ibn Malik, 2/348. He said: "This is how it is in my copy, in the handwriting of Hafs ibn 'Umar ibn al-Zubayr. I think 'al-Zubayr' is an error by the transmitter, since it is Hafs ibn 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Talhah al-Ansari, the nephew of Anas ibn Malik. If that is so, the hadith is sahih." He then said: "Abu Ya'qub Ishaq ibn Ibrahim also transmitted this hadith in his Tafsir as a mursal report." al-Haythami cited it from the narration of Anas and said: "al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Saghir and al-Awsat from his shaykh Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Bahili al-Basri, who is extremely weak." See Majma' al-Zawa'id 7/40. Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his Tafsir 2/488–489 from the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim and said: "This is a strange hadith containing a nakarah (a disavowed element)." al-Suyuti added its attribution to Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Faraj ba'd al-Shiddah, to Abu al-Shaykh, to Ibn Mardawayh, and to al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman. See al-Durr al-Manthur 4/574.]]

It is also reported that after that, when he had eaten lunch, he would order someone to call out: "Whoever wants lunch, let him come to Ya'qub." And when he broke his fast, he would order someone to call out: "Whoever wants to break his fast, let him come to Ya'qub." So he would eat lunch and dinner with the poor. [[See the previous note.]] From Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Allah the Exalted revealed to Ya'qub: "Do you know why I punished you and kept Yusuf away from you for eighty years?" He said: "No, my God." He said: "Because you roasted a young goat and withheld from your neighbour, and you ate and did not feed him."

It is also reported that the cause of Ya'qub's trial was that he slaughtered a calf in front of its mother while she was lowing. [[See Zad al-Masir by Ibn al-Jawzi 4/275.]] Wahb, al-Suddi and others said: Jibril came to Yusuf, peace be upon him, in the prison and said: "Do you recognise me, O truthful one?" He said: "I see a pure form and a good fragrance."

He said: "I am the messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and I am the Trustworthy Spirit."

He said: "Then what brought you into the place of the sinners, when you are the purest of the pure and the chief of those brought near [and the trustee of the Lord of the worlds]? [[Omitted in "B" (one of the manuscripts).]]"

He said: "Do you not know, O Yusuf, that Allah the Exalted purifies houses by the purity of the prophets, and that the land they enter is the purest of lands, and that Allah the Exalted has purified the prison and its surroundings through you? O purest of the pure and son of the righteous, sincere ones."

He said: "How can I claim the name of the truthful, when you count me among the sincere and pure, though I have been placed in the place of the sinners and named with the name of the wicked?"

Jibril said: "Because your heart was not seduced, and you did not obey your mistress in disobeying your Lord. For this reason Allah named you among the truthful, counted you among the sincere, and joined you to your righteous fathers."

Yusuf said: "Do you have knowledge of Ya'qub, O Trustworthy Spirit?"

He said: "Yes. Allah granted him beautiful patience, and tested him with grief over you, so he is *kazim* (one who suppresses his grief)."

He said: "How great is his grief?"

He said: "The grief of seventy bereaved mothers."

He said: "What reward does he have for it, O Jibril?"

He said: "The reward of one hundred martyrs."

He said: "Do you think I will meet him?"

He said: "Yes." So Yusuf's soul was content, and he said: "I do not mind what I have suffered if I see him." [[Reported from both of them by al-Tabari in his Tafsir 16/229–231. Wahb narrates many Isra'iliyyat (narrations from Jewish and Christian sources), and the narration of al-Suddi is weak.]]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, meaning: I know from the life of Yusuf what you do not know.

It is reported that the Angel of Death visited Ya'qub and said to him: "O angel whose scent is good and whose form is beautiful, have you taken the soul of my son among the souls?" He said: "No." Ya'qub was calmed and hoped to see him, and he said: ﴿And I know that the dream of Yusuf is true, and that I and you will surely prostrate to him.﴾

Al-Suddi said: When his son told him about the conduct of the king, Ya'qub's soul was stirred and he hoped, and he said: "Perhaps it is Yusuf." He said: "O my sons, go and search for news of Yusuf and his brother." [[See the tafsir of al-Qurtubi 9/253. al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Saghir and al-Awsat from his shaykh Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Bahili, who is extremely weak. See Majma' al-Zawa'id 7/40.]]

It is reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid ibn Abi Farwah that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, wrote a letter to Yusuf, peace be upon him, when Binyamin was detained: "From Ya'qub, Israel of Allah, son of Ishaq the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Ibrahim the friend of Allah, [to the king of Egypt]. [[Omitted in "B".]] To proceed: We are a household upon whom afflictions have been decreed. As for my grandfather Ibrahim, his hands and feet were bound and he was thrown into the fire, but Allah made it cool and safe for him. As for my father, his hands and feet were bound and the knife was placed on his nape, so Allah ransomed him. As for me, I had a son who was the dearest of my children to me, and his brothers took him to the wilderness, then they brought me his shirt stained with blood and said: 'The wolf has eaten him.' So my eyes lost their sight [from weeping for him]. [[Omitted in "B".]] Then I had another son, who was his brother by the same mother, and I was consoled by him. You have detained him and claimed that he stole. We are a household that does not steal, and we do not beget a thief. So if you return him to me, well and good; otherwise I will pray against you a prayer that will reach the seventh of your offspring."

When Yusuf read the letter, he could not hold back his weeping, and his patience gave way, so he revealed himself, as we shall mention, if Allah the Exalted wills. [[Reported by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Abu al-Shaykh from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who is weak. See al-Durr al-Manthur 4/579.]]

If it is formed as a *fa'il* pattern, in the manner of nouns, it takes on what nouns take: dual, plural, masculine and feminine. See al-Tabari 16/222.]]

﴿Or you become among those who perish﴾, that is: among the dead.

﴿He said﴾: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, at that moment, when he saw their harshness: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾. *Al-batthu* is the most intense grief. It is named so because the one who has it cannot bear it until he *yuthbitahu*, that is, reveals it. Al-Hasan said: *bathhi* means my need.

It is reported that a neighbour of his came to Ya'qub and said: "O Ya'qub, why do I see you broken and worn out? You have not reached the age that your father reached." He said: "What has broken me and worn me down is the trial Allah has afflicted me with, the grief over Yusuf." Allah revealed to him: "O Ya'qub, do you complain to My creatures?" He said: "O Lord, it was a sin I committed, so forgive it for me." He said: "I have forgiven it for you." After that, whenever he was asked, he would say: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾. [[Reported by al-Tabari in his Tafsir 16/227–228 from Talhah ibn Musarrif al-Yami, as a statement of his (mawquf). In the original it is "al-Iyami," and the form "al-Yami" is taken from Tahdhib al-Tahdhib, where he is described as a Kufan, learned reciter, of the fifth generation.]]

It is also reported that he was asked: "O Ya'qub, what took away your sight and bent your back?" He said: "My weeping for Yusuf took away my sight, and my grief for his brother bent my back." So Allah revealed to him: "Do you complain about Me? By My might and My majesty, I will not remove what is upon you until you call upon Me."

At that point he said: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾. Then Allah revealed to him: "By My might and My majesty, if they were both dead I would have brought them out for you. But I was displeased with you because you slaughtered a sheep, and a poor man stood at your door, and you did not give him any of it. The dearest of My creatures to Me are the prophets, then the poor. So prepare food and invite the poor to it."

So he prepared food and then said: "Whoever is fasting, let him break his fast tonight at the household of Ya'qub." [[Reported by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak from Anas ibn Malik, 2/348. He said: "This is how it is in my copy, in the handwriting of Hafs ibn 'Umar ibn al-Zubayr. I think 'al-Zubayr' is an error by the transmitter, since it is Hafs ibn 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Talhah al-Ansari, the nephew of Anas ibn Malik. If that is so, the hadith is sahih." He then said: "Abu Ya'qub Ishaq ibn Ibrahim also transmitted this hadith in his Tafsir as a mursal report." al-Haythami cited it from the narration of Anas and said: "al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Saghir and al-Awsat from his shaykh Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Bahili al-Basri, who is extremely weak." See Majma' al-Zawa'id 7/40. Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his Tafsir 2/488–489 from the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim and said: "This is a strange hadith containing a nakarah (a disavowed element)." al-Suyuti added its attribution to Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Faraj ba'd al-Shiddah, to Abu al-Shaykh, to Ibn Mardawayh, and to al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman. See al-Durr al-Manthur 4/574.]]

It is also reported that after that, when he had eaten lunch, he would order someone to call out: "Whoever wants lunch, let him come to Ya'qub." And when he broke his fast, he would order someone to call out: "Whoever wants to break his fast, let him come to Ya'qub." So he would eat lunch and dinner with the poor. [[See the previous note.]] From Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Allah the Exalted revealed to Ya'qub: "Do you know why I punished you and kept Yusuf away from you for eighty years?" He said: "No, my God." He said: "Because you roasted a young goat and withheld from your neighbour, and you ate and did not feed him."

It is also reported that the cause of Ya'qub's trial was that he slaughtered a calf in front of its mother while she was lowing. [[See Zad al-Masir by Ibn al-Jawzi 4/275.]] Wahb, al-Suddi and others said: Jibril came to Yusuf, peace be upon him, in the prison and said: "Do you recognise me, O truthful one?" He said: "I see a pure form and a good fragrance."

He said: "I am the messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and I am the Trustworthy Spirit."

He said: "Then what brought you into the place of the sinners, when you are the purest of the pure and the chief of those brought near [and the trustee of the Lord of the worlds]? [[Omitted in "B" (one of the manuscripts).]]"

He said: "Do you not know, O Yusuf, that Allah the Exalted purifies houses by the purity of the prophets, and that the land they enter is the purest of lands, and that Allah the Exalted has purified the prison and its surroundings through you? O purest of the pure and son of the righteous, sincere ones."

He said: "How can I claim the name of the truthful, when you count me among the sincere and pure, though I have been placed in the place of the sinners and named with the name of the wicked?"

Jibril said: "Because your heart was not seduced, and you did not obey your mistress in disobeying your Lord. For this reason Allah named you among the truthful, counted you among the sincere, and joined you to your righteous fathers."

Yusuf said: "Do you have knowledge of Ya'qub, O Trustworthy Spirit?"

He said: "Yes. Allah granted him beautiful patience, and tested him with grief over you, so he is *kazim* (one who suppresses his grief)."

He said: "How great is his grief?"

He said: "The grief of seventy bereaved mothers."

He said: "What reward does he have for it, O Jibril?"

He said: "The reward of one hundred martyrs."

He said: "Do you think I will meet him?"

He said: "Yes." So Yusuf's soul was content, and he said: "I do not mind what I have suffered if I see him." [[Reported from both of them by al-Tabari in his Tafsir 16/229–231. Wahb narrates many Isra'iliyyat (narrations from Jewish and Christian sources), and the narration of al-Suddi is weak.]]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, meaning: I know from the life of Yusuf what you do not know.

It is reported that the Angel of Death visited Ya'qub and said to him: "O angel whose scent is good and whose form is beautiful, have you taken the soul of my son among the souls?" He said: "No." Ya'qub was calmed and hoped to see him, and he said: ﴿And I know that the dream of Yusuf is true, and that I and you will surely prostrate to him.﴾

Al-Suddi said: When his son told him about the conduct of the king, Ya'qub's soul was stirred and he hoped, and he said: "Perhaps it is Yusuf." He said: "O my sons, go and search for news of Yusuf and his brother." [[See the tafsir of al-Qurtubi 9/253. al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Saghir and al-Awsat from his shaykh Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Bahili, who is extremely weak. See Majma' al-Zawa'id 7/40.]]

It is reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid ibn Abi Farwah that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, wrote a letter to Yusuf, peace be upon him, when Binyamin was detained: "From Ya'qub, Israel of Allah, son of Ishaq the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Ibrahim the friend of Allah, [to the king of Egypt]. [[Omitted in "B".]] To proceed: We are a household upon whom afflictions have been decreed. As for my grandfather Ibrahim, his hands and feet were bound and he was thrown into the fire, but Allah made it cool and safe for him. As for my father, his hands and feet were bound and the knife was placed on his nape, so Allah ransomed him. As for me, I had a son who was the dearest of my children to me, and his brothers took him to the wilderness, then they brought me his shirt stained with blood and said: 'The wolf has eaten him.' So my eyes lost their sight [from weeping for him]. [[Omitted in "B".]] Then I had another son, who was his brother by the same mother, and I was consoled by him. You have detained him and claimed that he stole. We are a household that does not steal, and we do not beget a thief. So if you return him to me, well and good; otherwise I will pray against you a prayer that will reach the seventh of your offspring."

When Yusuf read the letter, he could not hold back his weeping, and his patience gave way, so he revealed himself, as we shall mention, if Allah the Exalted wills. [[Reported by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Abu al-Shaykh from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who is weak. See al-Durr al-Manthur 4/579.]]

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 87–88:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿O my sons, go and search (fatahassasu)﴾ — take news and seek information — ﴿about Yusuf and his brother﴾. The word tahassus, with ḥā' or with jīm, the two do not differ greatly from each other, except that tahassus with ḥā' is used for good and with jīm for evil. Tahassus is seeking a thing through the senses (al-ḥāssah). Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is "seek out." ﴿And do not despair (tay'asu)﴾ — do not lose hope — ﴿of the comfort (rawḥ) of Allah﴾, that is, of the mercy of Allah. It was also said: of the relief (faraj) of Allah.

﴿Indeed, none despairs of the comfort of Allah except the disbelieving people.﴾

﴿So when they entered upon him﴾ — there is an omission here, its implied sense being: they set out returning to Egypt until they reached it, then they entered upon Yusuf, peace be upon him.

﴿They said: O Chief (al-ʿAzīz), adversity has touched us and our family﴾ — that is, hardship and hunger — ﴿and we have come with meager merchandise (biḍāʿah muzjāh)﴾ — that is, little and poor, defective goods, not accepted for the price of food except with leniency from the seller concerning it. The root of izjāʾ is driving and pushing. It was also said: the merchandise is called muzjāh because it is not current, and it is only accepted by the pusher of its taker.

They differed concerning it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was poor dirhams, debased coins (zuyūf) [[The dirhams in which adulteration and inferiority appeared.]].

It was said: it was worn-out sacks and ropes [[al-khalq: the worn-out. al-gharāʾir: plural of gharāra, a container of burlap or the like in which wheat and the like is put, larger than the jawāliq. See al-Muʿjam al-Wasīt: 2/648.]].

It was said: it was goods of the Bedouins, of wool and dried curd (aqiṭ).

al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: it was the green grain (al-ḥabbah al-khaḍrāʾ).

It was said: it was of sawīq al-muql [[al-muql: the fruit of the doum palm, which resembles the date palm.]].

It was said: it was leather goods and sandals [[al-Ṭabari said concerning "and we have come with meager merchandise": dirhams, or a currency not accepted for the price of food except from one who is lenient in it... The people of interpretation differed in the explanation of its meaning, though their explanations are close in meaning. Al-Tafsir: 16/234, 235.]].

﴿So give us full measure⁠﴾ — that is, give us what you used to give us before, at the good and full price.

﴿And be charitable to us⁠﴾ — that is, show favour to us by the difference between the good price and the poor one, and do not diminish us. This is the saying of most exegetes.

Ibn Jurayj and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "and be charitable to us by returning our brother to us" [[al-Ṭabari, commenting on what Ibn Jurayj mentioned: this saying, though it has a basis, is not the preferred view... because charity in the customary usage of the Arabs is only giving a person in need some of one's possessions seeking Allah's reward for it, though every good deed is charity. So directing the interpretation of Allah's speech to the more prevalent meaning in the speech of those in whose tongue the Qur'an was revealed is more fitting and more proper.]].

﴿Indeed, Allah rewards (yajzī) — recompenses — ﴿the charitable⁠﴾.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they did not say "Indeed Allah will reward you," because they did not know that he was a believer.

Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah was asked: Was charity forbidden to any of the prophets other than our Prophet, peace be upon him? Sufyan said: Did you not hear His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And be charitable to us; indeed Allah rewards the charitable⁠﴾ [[Narrated by al-Ṭabari: 16/242. Ibn ʿAtiyyah rejected it with the hadith ("We, the company of prophets, charity is not lawful for us"). See al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz: 8/63.]], meaning that charity was lawful for them.

It is narrated that al-Ḥasan heard a man say: "O Allah, be charitable to me," and he said: Indeed Allah does not give charity; rather, only one who seeks reward gives charity. Say: "O Allah, give me, or show favour to me." [[Mujahid said the same; he was asked: Is it disliked for a man to say in his supplication "O Allah, be charitable to me"? He said: Yes, charity is only for one who seeks reward. See al-Ṭabari: 16/243; al-Durr al-Manthur: 4/577.]]
