Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 89–90:

﴿He said: "Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?"﴾ They differed concerning the reason that moved Yusuf to this statement. Ibn Ishaq said: "It was mentioned to me that when they spoke to him with these words, tenderness overcame him and his tears flowed (arfada al-dam'u wa-tarfada: it descended and flowed),[[Ibn Ishaq's report is cited by al-Tabari in his Tafsir: 16/243.]] so he revealed what he had been concealing from them."

Al-Kalbi said: "He said that only when he related to his brothers that Malik ibn Dhu'r had said: 'I found a boy in a well, with such-and-such a condition, and I bought him for such-and-such dirhams.' They said: 'O King, we sold that boy.' Yusuf was angered by this, and he ordered that they be killed, so they took them away to kill them. Yahudha turned back, saying: 'Ya'qub used to grieve and weep for the loss of one of us until his sight failed; how then will it be when the killing of all his sons reaches him?' Then they said to him: 'If you do that, then send our belongings to our father, for he is in such-and-such a place.' At that point he had mercy on them and wept, and said that statement.'"[[Narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. See Zad al-Masir by Ibn al-Jawzi: 4/279.]]

It was also said: he said it when he read his father's letter to him, and he could not restrain his weeping, so he said: "Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you separated them, and did what you did, when you were ignorant of what Yusuf's affair would lead to?" It was also said: "Sinners and disobedient." Al-Hasan said: "When you were young, and you had the ignorance of youth."

If it is asked: how did he say "what you did to Yusuf and his brother," when what they had done to his brother was not something they had striven to imprison him for? It is answered: they had said to him regarding the measuring cup, "There will always be a calamity for us," and it was also said: "We have not seen from you, O sons of Rachel, any good." It was also said: since the two were from one mother, they kept harming him after the loss of Yusuf.

﴿They said: "Are you indeed Yusuf?"﴾ Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read "innaka" as a statement; the others read it as a question.

Ibn Ishaq said: Yusuf was speaking from behind a veil, and when Yusuf said, "Do you know what you did," he uncovered the cover from them and lifted the curtain, and they recognized him.

Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn Abbas: when he said this statement, Yusuf smiled, and they saw his front teeth like strung pearls, so they likened him to Yusuf and said, as a question: "Are you indeed Yusuf?"

Ata reported from Ibn Abbas: the brothers of Yusuf did not recognize him until he removed the crown from his head. He had a mark on his horn, and Ya'qub had a similar one, and Ishaq had a similar one, and Sarah had a similar one, a mark like a mole. So they recognized him and said: "Are you indeed Yusuf?"

It was also said: they said it by way of supposition until, ﴿He said: "I am Yusuf, and this is my brother"﴾, Binyamin, ﴿"Allah has indeed been gracious to us"﴾, meaning He bestowed His favor upon us by bringing us together.

﴿"Indeed, whoever fears Allah"﴾ by performing the obligations and avoiding sins, ﴿"and is patient"﴾ regarding what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden to him. Ibn Abbas said: he fears adultery and is patient about celibacy. Mujahid said: he fears disobedience and is patient under imprisonment. ﴿"Then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers."﴾

﴿He said: "Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?"﴾ They differed concerning the reason that moved Yusuf to this statement. Ibn Ishaq said: "It was mentioned to me that when they spoke to him with these words, tenderness overcame him and his tears flowed (arfada al-dam'u wa-tarfada: it descended and flowed),[[Ibn Ishaq's report is cited by al-Tabari in his Tafsir: 16/243.]] so he revealed what he had been concealing from them."

He had a mark on his horn, and Ya'qub had a similar one, and Ishaq had a similar one, and Sarah had a similar one, a mark like a mole. So they recognized him and said: "Are you indeed Yusuf?"

It was also said: they said it by way of supposition until, ﴿He said: "I am Yusuf, and this is my brother"﴾, Binyamin, ﴿"Allah has indeed been gracious to us"﴾, meaning He bestowed His favor upon us by bringing us together.

Ibn Abbas said: he fears adultery and is patient about celibacy. Mujahid said: he fears disobedience and is patient under imprisonment. ﴿"Then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers."﴾

﴿They said﴾, apologising: ﴿By God, God has certainly preferred you over us﴾, meaning: God chose you and favoured you over us; ﴿and we were certainly sinners﴾, meaning: in our treatment of you we were nothing but mistaken and guilty. It is said: khati'a (خَطِئَ) khit'an means he did it deliberately, whereas akhta'a (أَخْطَأَ) means he did it without intent. [[Al-Raghib al-Isfahani (d. 502 AH) says in his book "al-Mufradat fi Gharib al-Qur'an" (p. 151): "Al-khata' (error) is deviating from the right course, and it has several kinds. The first: one intends what is not good to intend and then does it; this is the complete error for which a person is held accountable. It is said: khati'a yakhta'u khit'an and khita'a; God the Exalted said: (And we were certainly sinners). The second: one intends what is good to do, but what happens from him is contrary to what he intended; it is said: akhta'a ikhta'an, so he is mukhti'. Here he was right in intention but wrong in action, and this is what is meant by the Prophet's saying (peace be upon him): 'Error and forgetfulness have been lifted from my community'. The third: one intends what is not good to do and it happens to turn out otherwise; this one is mistaken in intention and correct in action, so he is blamed for his intention and not praised for his deed..." See also: Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/110, 6/134, 16/245.]].

﴿He said﴾ — Yusuf, who was forbearing — ﴿"No reproach shall be upon you today. God will forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ Meaning: no rebuke shall be upon you today, and I shall not mention your sin to you after today.

When Yusuf made himself known to them, he asked them about his father, saying: "What has my father done after me?" They said: "His eyes have gone white," so he gave them his shirt and said:

﴿"Go with this shirt of mine and cast it upon the face of my father; he will come back seeing."﴾ Meaning: he will return seeing. It was also said: "He will come to me seeing," because he had prayed for that.

Al-Hasan said: He did not know that he would return seeing except after God, Mighty and Majestic, informed him.

Al-Dahhak said: That shirt was woven from the cloth of Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 94:**

﴿When the caravan set out﴾, i.e., it departed from the land of Egypt heading toward Canaan. ﴿Their father said﴾, i.e., Ya'qub (Jacob) said to the sons of his sons, ﴿Indeed, I detect the scent of Yusuf (Joseph)﴾.

It is narrated that the *sabā* (the east wind) asked its Lord for permission to bring Ya'qub the scent of Yusuf before the bearer of good news reached him.

Mujahid said: Ya'qub perceived the scent of Yusuf from a distance of three days' journey. It is related from Ibn Abbas: from a distance of eight [[In "B": three.]] nights' journey.

Al-Hasan said: there were eighty *farsakh* (a unit of distance, roughly three miles) between them. [[See: al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya by Ibn Kathir: 1/216.]]

It is also said: a wind blew and stirred the shirt, so it carried the scent of the shirt to Ya'qub, and he found the scent of Paradise. He knew that there is nothing on earth of the scent of Paradise except what came from that shirt. Therefore he said: ﴿Indeed, I detect the scent of Yusuf﴾.

﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾: *tufannidun* means you would deem me foolish. It is related from Ibn Abbas: you would deem me ignorant. Al-Dahhak said: you would consider me aged, so you would say, "He is an old man who has become senile and lost his mind." It is also said: you would consider me weak. Abu Ubayda said: you would consider me astray. The root of *fanad* is corruption.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verses 95–98:**

﴿They said﴾, that is, the children of his children: ﴿"By God, you are surely in your old error"﴾, that is, your old mistake of remembering Joseph; do not forget him. Ḍalāl (error) is departing from the path of what is right. They believed that Joseph had died, and they saw that Jacob had become constantly occupied with mentioning him.

﴿Then when the bearer of good news came﴾, who was the one announcing the news about Joseph. Ibn Mas'ud said: the bearer of good news came ahead of the caravan. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was Yahudha (Judah).

al-Suddi said: Yahudha said, "I took the shirt, stained with blood, to Jacob and told him that the wolf had eaten Joseph. Today I will go to him with the shirt and inform him that his son is alive, so that I may gladden him as I once grieved him." [See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/259.]

Ibn 'Abbas said: Yahudha carried it and went out barefoot and bareheaded, running, with seven loaves of bread, and he had not finished eating them by the time he reached his father. The distance was eighty farsakh.

It is also said: the bearer of good news was Malik ibn Dh'ur.

﴿He cast it upon his face﴾, that is, the bearer cast Joseph's shirt upon the face of Jacob, ﴿and he regained his sight﴾, meaning he returned to sight after having been blind, and his strength returned after weakness, his youth after old age, and his joy after sorrow.

﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that I know from God what you do not know?"﴾ Concerning the living Joseph, and that God would reunite us.

It is related that he asked the bearer of good news, "How did you leave Joseph?" He said, "He is the king of Egypt." Jacob said, "What do I want with kingship? On what religion did you leave him?" He said, "On the religion of Islam." He said, "Now the blessing is complete." [Ibn al-Jawzi in Zad al-Masir (4/286) said: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated it from Sufyan. al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (4/583) attributed it to Ibn Abi Hatim from al-Hasan as a statement of his own (mawquf).]

﴿They said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for our sins; indeed, we were sinners"﴾, that is, guilty.

﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you"﴾. Most of the exegetes said: he delayed the supplication until the last part of the night, which is the time when God, exalted is He, says: ﴿"Is there any who calls upon Me, that I may respond to him?"﴾ [This refers to the authentic hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "Our Lord, blessed and exalted, descends every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains, and says: Whoever calls upon Me, I will answer him; whoever asks of Me, I will give him; whoever seeks My forgiveness, I will forgive him." Related by al-Bukhari in Tahajjud, chapter on supplication and prayer in the last part of the night: 3/29, and by Muslim in Prayer of the Travellers, chapter on encouragement to supplication and remembrance in the last part of the night, no. (758): 1/521.] When Jacob reached the appointed time, he stood in prayer in the last part of the night. When he finished, he raised his hands to God, mighty and majestic, and said: "O God, forgive me my grief over Joseph and my lack of patience concerning him, and forgive my sons for what they did to their brother Joseph." God revealed to him: "I have indeed forgiven you and all of them."

From 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: ﴿I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you﴾ means on the night of Friday. [Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report: "He will say, until the night of Friday comes." This is the statement of Jacob's son to his sons. Tafsir: 16/262; for its takhrij see Mahmud Shakir's annotation on it. Ibn Kathir said in al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya (1/217): "This is strange from this route, and its being traced to the Prophet is questionable; it is more likely to be a statement of Ibn 'Abbas only (mawquf)."] Wahb said: he would ask forgiveness for them every Friday night for more than twenty years.

Tawus said: he delayed the supplication until the last part of the night of Friday, and it coincided with the night of 'Ashura'. [See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/263.] From al-Sha'bi, who said: "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you": "I will ask Joseph: if he pardons you, I will ask my Lord to forgive you." [Same reference.] ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.

It is related that Joseph had sent with the bearer of good news to Jacob two hundred riding beasts and abundant provisions, so that they might bring Jacob, his family and his children. Jacob prepared to set out for Egypt, and they departed, and they were seventy-two people, men and women. Masruq said: they were ninety-three. When he drew near to Egypt, Joseph spoke to the king who was above him, and Joseph went out with the king in four thousand troops, and the people of Egypt rode with them to welcome Jacob. Jacob was walking, leaning on Yahudha, and he looked at the horses and the people and said: "O Yahudha, is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, this is your son." When each of them drew near to the other, Joseph went to begin with the greeting, but Gabriel said: "No, until Jacob begins with the greeting." Jacob said: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows." [Most of these reports are taken from the People of the Book. See: al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya by Ibn Kathir: 1/217–218.]

It is also related that the two of them dismounted and embraced. al-Thawri said: when Jacob and Joseph, peace be upon them both, met, each of them embraced the other and they wept. Joseph said, "O father, you have wept until your sight has gone. Do you not know that the Resurrection will gather us?" He said, "Yes, my son, but I feared that your religion would be taken from you, and that I would be separated from you." [See: al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/347.]

He said, "Yes, my son, but I feared that your religion would be taken from you, and that I would be separated from you." [See: al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/347.]

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verses 95–98:**

﴿They said﴾, that is, the children of his children: ﴿"By God, you are surely in your old error"﴾, that is, your old mistake of remembering Joseph; do not forget him. Ḍalāl (error) is departing from the path of what is right. They believed that Joseph had died, and they saw that Jacob had become constantly occupied with mentioning him.

﴿Then when the bearer of good news came﴾, who was the one announcing the news about Joseph. Ibn Mas'ud said: the bearer of good news came ahead of the caravan. Ibn 'Abbas said: he was Yahudha (Judah).

al-Suddi said: Yahudha said, "I took the shirt, stained with blood, to Jacob and told him that the wolf had eaten Joseph. Today I will go to him with the shirt and inform him that his son is alive, so that I may gladden him as I once grieved him." [See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/259.]

Ibn 'Abbas said: Yahudha carried it and went out barefoot and bareheaded, running, with seven loaves of bread, and he had not finished eating them by the time he reached his father. The distance was eighty farsakh.

It is also said: the bearer of good news was Malik ibn Dh'ur.

﴿He cast it upon his face﴾, that is, the bearer cast Joseph's shirt upon the face of Jacob, ﴿and he regained his sight﴾, meaning he returned to sight after having been blind, and his strength returned after weakness, his youth after old age, and his joy after sorrow.

﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that I know from God what you do not know?"﴾ Concerning the living Joseph, and that God would reunite us.

It is related that he asked the bearer of good news, "How did you leave Joseph?" He said, "He is the king of Egypt." Jacob said, "What do I want with kingship? On what religion did you leave him?" He said, "On the religion of Islam." He said, "Now the blessing is complete." [Ibn al-Jawzi in Zad al-Masir (4/286) said: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated it from Sufyan. al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (4/583) attributed it to Ibn Abi Hatim from al-Hasan as a statement of his own (mawquf).]

﴿They said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for our sins; indeed, we were sinners"﴾, that is, guilty.

﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you"﴾. Most of the exegetes said: he delayed the supplication until the last part of the night, which is the time when God, exalted is He, says: ﴿"Is there any who calls upon Me, that I may respond to him?"﴾ [This refers to the authentic hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "Our Lord, blessed and exalted, descends every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains, and says: Whoever calls upon Me, I will answer him; whoever asks of Me, I will give him; whoever seeks My forgiveness, I will forgive him." Related by al-Bukhari in Tahajjud, chapter on supplication and prayer in the last part of the night: 3/29, and by Muslim in Prayer of the Travellers, chapter on encouragement to supplication and remembrance in the last part of the night, no. (758): 1/521.] When Jacob reached the appointed time, he stood in prayer in the last part of the night. When he finished, he raised his hands to God, mighty and majestic, and said: "O God, forgive me my grief over Joseph and my lack of patience concerning him, and forgive my sons for what they did to their brother Joseph." God revealed to him: "I have indeed forgiven you and all of them."

From 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: ﴿I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you﴾ means on the night of Friday. [Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report: "He will say, until the night of Friday comes." This is the statement of Jacob's son to his sons. Tafsir: 16/262; for its takhrij see Mahmud Shakir's annotation on it. Ibn Kathir said in al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya (1/217): "This is strange from this route, and its being traced to the Prophet is questionable; it is more likely to be a statement of Ibn 'Abbas only (mawquf)."] Wahb said: he would ask forgiveness for them every Friday night for more than twenty years.

Tawus said: he delayed the supplication until the last part of the night of Friday, and it coincided with the night of 'Ashura'. [See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/263.] From al-Sha'bi, who said: "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you": "I will ask Joseph: if he pardons you, I will ask my Lord to forgive you." [Same reference.] ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.

It is related that Joseph had sent with the bearer of good news to Jacob two hundred riding beasts and abundant provisions, so that they might bring Jacob, his family and his children. Jacob prepared to set out for Egypt, and they departed, and they were seventy-two people, men and women. Masruq said: they were ninety-three. When he drew near to Egypt, Joseph spoke to the king who was above him, and Joseph went out with the king in four thousand troops, and the people of Egypt rode with them to welcome Jacob. Jacob was walking, leaning on Yahudha, and he looked at the horses and the people and said: "O Yahudha, is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, this is your son." When each of them drew near to the other, Joseph went to begin with the greeting, but Gabriel said: "No, until Jacob begins with the greeting." Jacob said: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows." [Most of these reports are taken from the People of the Book. See: al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya by Ibn Kathir: 1/217–218.]

It is also related that the two of them dismounted and embraced. al-Thawri said: when Jacob and Joseph, peace be upon them both, met, each of them embraced the other and they wept. Joseph said, "O father, you have wept until your sight has gone. Do you not know that the Resurrection will gather us?" He said, "Yes, my son, but I feared that your religion would be taken from you, and that I would be separated from you." [See: al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/347.]

﴿فَلَمَّا دَخَلُوا عَلَى يُوسُفَ آوَى إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ﴾ *"When they entered upon Joseph, he drew his parents close to him."* Ya'ni: ḍamma ilayhi (he took them to himself).

﴿أَبَوَيْهِ﴾ Most of the exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: they were his father and his maternal aunt (khalatuhu), Layya. His mother Rahil had died in childbirth with Binyamin [[Narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh from Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Tabari from al-Suddi. See al-Durr al-Manthur: 4/587-588; al-Tabari: 16/267.]].

Al-Hasan said: they were his father and his mother, and she was alive [[Narrated by al-Tabari from Ibn Ishaq, and he said: "It is more correct, because that is the most common usage among people and what is understood by 'parents' among them, unless it is established, by a proof that must be accepted, that Joseph's mother had died before that; in that case it is to be accepted." See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/267; al-Muharrar al-Wajiz of Ibn Atiyyah: 8/79.]].

In some tafsirs (exegetical works) it is related that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brought his mother back to life so that she came to Egypt with Ya'qub. [See: al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/347. Al-Alusi said (13/57): "The apparent view is that this was not established; had such a thing been established, it would have been well known."]

﴿وَقَالَ ادْخُلُوا مِصْرَ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ آمِنِينَ﴾ *"And he said: Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security."*

If it is said: He has said "When they entered upon Joseph, he drew his parents to himself," so how can he say "Enter Egypt" after it has been reported that they had entered it? And what is the purpose of this exception (istithna') when entry has already taken place?

It is said: Joseph said this to them only when he met them before they entered Egypt. In the verse there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and the exception refers back to the seeking of forgiveness, which is from the words of Ya'qub to his sons: "I shall ask my Lord to forgive you, if Allah wills" [[Al-Tabari explained this, saying: "... The exegetes differed about this. Some said: Ya'qub entered upon Joseph together with his children, and Joseph drew his parents to himself before they entered Egypt. They said: That is because Joseph met his father to honour him before he entered Egypt, and he drew him to himself, then said to him and to those with him: (Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security) before entering... This is the view of al-Suddi. Others said: rather, his saying (if Allah wills) is an exception from Ya'qub's saying to his sons: (I shall ask my Lord to forgive you). He said: This is of what is delayed in meaning and placed earlier. They said: The meaning of the speech is: He said: I shall ask my Lord to forgive you, if Allah wills, indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. Then when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his parents to himself, and said: Enter Egypt, and he raised his parents... This is the view of Ibn Jurayj. Then he preferred the first view, saying: "The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is what al-Suddi said, namely that Joseph said that to his parents and to those of their children and families who were with them before they entered Egypt, when he met them, because that is so in the apparent sense of the revelation. There is no indication that supports what Ibn Jurayj said, and there is no justification for moving any part of the Book of Allah from its place or delaying it from its position except with clear proof." See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/264-266. The hafiz Ibn Kathir well affirmed al-Tabari's refutation of Ibn Jurayj and his preference for the view of al-Suddi, then said (2/491): "And what prevents it from being that he said to them, after they had entered upon him and he had drawn them to himself: Enter Egypt, and what is implied is: Settle in Egypt, if Allah wills, in security, that is, from what you were in of hardship and famine..." This interpretation was mentioned by Ibn Atiyyah (8/79), who said in explaining the words of the Most High (Enter Egypt): "its meaning: Establish yourselves, settle and remain, for they had already entered upon him." Then he mentioned the view of al-Suddi, and said (8/80): "This exception is what the Qur'an encourages a person to say concerning everything he will carry out in the future." He mentioned the view of Ibn Jurayj and said: "There is weakness in this interpretation." See also: Tafsir al-Qurtubi (9/263).]].

It was also said: The exception refers to security from the permission (jiwaz), because they would not enter Egypt before him except with permission (jiwaz) from its kings. He says: secure from the permission, if Allah the Most High wills [[In al-Zad al-Masir it is written with the letter ra' (bi'l-ra'). Perhaps this is more fitting.]], as He said: ﴿لَتَدْخُلُنَّ الْمَسْجِدَ الْحَرَامَ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ آمِنِينَ﴾ *"You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security"* [al-Fath: 27]. [[In al-Kashshaf: the will is connected to the entry qualified by security, because the aim is that they be described by security in their entry; it is as if it were said: "Be safe and secure in your entering, if Allah wills..." The estimated meaning is: Enter Egypt in security, if Allah wills you enter in security, so the response (jaza') is omitted because the speech indicates it. Then the response clause was interposed between the state (hal) and its owner (dhu al-hal). Al-Tibi said: It is as if he indicated by his saying "it is as if it were said..." etc. that the structure contains the meaning of supplication. See: al-Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari: 2/277; Ruh al-Ma'ani of al-Alusi: 13/57.]]

It was also said: "in" (in) here has the meaning of "idh" (since/when), meaning: "since Allah willed", as in His saying: ﴿وَأَنْتُمُ الْأَعْلَوْنَ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ *"You will be the superior if you are believers"* [Al 'Imran: 139], i.e., "since you are believers" [[From this four views are obtained, which Ibn al-Jawzi summarised in Zad al-Masir (4/289): First: that there is inversion and reordering in the speech. Second: that the exception returns to the security. Within this there are two views: one, that he did not trust that the calamities would turn away from them; the other, that people used to fear the kings of Egypt in past times, so they would not enter except under their protection. Third: that it refers to entering Egypt, because he said this when he met them. Fourth: that "in" means "idh".]].

﴿وَرَفَعَ أَبَوَيْهِ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ﴾ *"And he raised his parents upon the throne."* Ya'ni: 'ala al-sarir (upon the couch): he seated them. Al-raf' (raising) is moving to a high place.

﴿وَخَرُّوا لَهُ سُجَّدًا﴾ *"And they fell down before him in prostration."* Ya'ni: Ya'qub, his maternal aunt and his brothers.

The greeting of people in that time was prostration (sujud), and by prostration is not meant placing the foreheads on the ground; it is only bowing (inhina') and humility [[Said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan. See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/265; Zad al-Masir 4/290.]].

It was also said: They placed their foreheads on the ground, and that was by way of greeting and honouring, not by way of worship. That was permissible in earlier nations, then it was abrogated (nusikha, naskh) in this law [[Said by al-Thawri, al-Dahhak and others, as related by al-Qurtubi: 9/265, and al-Tabari also related it from al-Dahhak and Sufyan al-Thawri. They said: prostration was a greeting among them. Ibn Zayd said: that prostration was because of his nobility, as the angels prostrated to Adam for his nobility, not a prostration of worship. Al-Tabari said: What is meant is that this was from them towards creation, not by way of worship. Something that shows that this has always been a habit of people from ancient times before Islam, not as worship from some to others, is the saying of A'sha Bani Tha'labah: "When he came to us after the drowsiness of sleep, / we prostrated to him and raised 'Amar." See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/270.]].

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: its meaning: they fell down prostrate to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, before Joseph [[Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: He raised his parents upon the couch, and they prostrated to him, and his brothers prostrated to him. This contradicts what al-Baghawi mentioned. Al-Naqqash said: This is an error; the pronoun refers back to Joseph, peace be upon him, because of the Most High's saying at the beginning of the surah: (I saw them prostrating to me), and their greeting was that the lowly prostrate to the noble, and the young to the elder. See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/269; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/264.]]. The first is more correct [[The exegetes agreed that that prostration, in whatever manner it was, was only a greeting, not worship. Qatadah said: This was the greeting of kings among them, and Allah gave this community the greeting of the people of Paradise, peace. Al-Qurtubi observed that this abrogated practice had become a custom in his time among some people, so he censured them, saying: "This bowing and bending which has been abrogated for us has become a custom in the land of Egypt and among the non-Arabs, and likewise standing for one another; so that if one of them does not stand for another, he feels in himself as if he is not regarded and has no worth; and likewise when they meet, some of them bow to others, a continuous custom and a settled inheritance, especially when rulers and leaders meet. They have turned away from the sunnah and have deviated from the sunnah." It is related that Anas ibn Malik said: We said: O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! Should some of us bow to others when we meet? He said: No. We said: Should some of us embrace others? He said: No. We said: Should some of us shake hands with others? He said: Yes (narrated by Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Tamhid). See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/265-266; cf. al-Muharrar al-Wajiz: 8/80; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/491-492.]].

﴿وَقَالَ﴾ Joseph, at that moment: ﴿يَا أَبَتِ هَذَا تَأْوِيلُ رُؤْيَايَ مِنْ قَبْلُ قَدْ جَعَلَهَا رَبِّي حَقًّا﴾ *"O my father! This is the interpretation of my dream from before; my Lord has made it true."* This is His saying: "Indeed I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."

﴿وَقَدْ أَحْسَنَ بِي﴾ *"And He was indeed good to me"* [my Lord, i.e.] [[Omitted from "A".]]: He bestowed favour upon me. ﴿إِذْ أَخْرَجَنِي مِنَ السِّجْنِ﴾ *"when He brought me out of the prison."* He did not say "out of the well" (al-jubb), although the well was a greater trial than the prison, out of courtesy (istikhdaman lil-karam), so that his brothers would not be ashamed after he had said to them: "No reproach upon you today." Also, because Allah's blessing upon him in bringing him out of prison was greater: after coming out of the well he went into slavery and bondage, and after coming out of prison he came to kingship. Also, because his falling into the well was due to the envy of his brothers, whereas in prison it was a recompense from Allah the Most High for a slip that had come from him.

﴿وَجَاءَ بِكُمْ مِنَ الْبَدْوِ﴾ *"and brought you from the desert."* Al-badw is a flat expanse of land inhabited by the people of livestock with their herds; they were people of the desert and of livestock. It is said: badā yabdū, when one goes out to the desert.

﴿مِنْ بَعْدِ أَنْ نَزَغَ﴾ *"after Satan had sown discord"* afsada (corrupted), ﴿الشَّيْطَانُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ إِخْوَتِي﴾ *"between me and my brothers"* through envy.

﴿إِنَّ رَبِّي لَطِيفٌ﴾ *"Indeed my Lord is Gentle"* ayy: possessor of gentleness, ﴿لِمَا يَشَاءُ﴾ *"toward whom He wills."* It was also said: its meaning is "to whomever He wills" [[In "B": li-man.]].

The reality of al-latif (the Gentle) is the One who conveys kindness to others with gentleness (bi'l-rifq) [[In "B": "that He conveys."]]. ﴿إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْعَلِيمُ الْحَكِيمُ﴾ *"Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."*

The historians (ahl al-tarikh) said: Ya'qub remained in Egypt with Joseph for twenty-four years, in the most enviable condition and the most pleasant life. Then he died in Egypt. When death came to him, he bequeathed to his son Joseph that he should carry his body until he buried him beside his father Ishaq. So Joseph did that, and went with him until he buried him in al-Sham (Syria), then he returned to Egypt.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, was carried in a coffin of teak to Bayt al-Maqdis, and that day coincided with the day on which al-Is died, and they were buried in one grave. They had been born in one womb, and their lifespan was one hundred and forty-seven years [[These reports are taken from the People of the Book, and historians have mentioned them together with other reports, and Allah knows best their soundness. The hafiz Ibn Kathir indicated this, indeed he said: "And among the People of the Book it is said that the age of Ya'qub ..." etc. See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/276; Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/363-364; al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya of Ibn Kathir: 1/220; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/492; al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti: 4/589-590.]].

When Allah the Most High had gathered Joseph's scattered family together, and he knew that the bounties of this world do not last, he asked Allah the Most High for a good end, and he said:

Second: that the exception returns to the security. Third: that it refers to entering Egypt, because he said this when he met them. Fourth: that "in" means "idh".]].

﴿وَرَفَعَ أَبَوَيْهِ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ﴾ *"And he raised his parents upon the throne."* Ya'ni: 'ala al-sarir (upon the couch): he seated them. Al-raf' (raising) is moving to a high place.

﴿وَخَرُّوا لَهُ سُجَّدًا﴾ *"And they fell down before him in prostration."* Ya'ni: Ya'qub, his maternal aunt and his brothers.

The greeting of people in that time was prostration (sujud), and by prostration is not meant placing the foreheads on the ground; it is only bowing (inhina') and humility [[Said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan. See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/265; Zad al-Masir 4/290.]].

It was also said: They placed their foreheads on the ground, and that was by way of greeting and honouring, not by way of worship. That was permissible in earlier nations, then it was abrogated (nusikha, naskh) in this law [[Said by al-Thawri, al-Dahhak and others, as related by al-Qurtubi: 9/265, and al-Tabari also related it from al-Dahhak and Sufyan al-Thawri. They said: prostration was a greeting among them. Ibn Zayd said: that prostration was because of his nobility, as the angels prostrated to Adam for his nobility, not a prostration of worship. Al-Tabari said: What is meant is that this was from them towards creation, not by way of worship. Something that shows that this has always been a habit of people from ancient times before Islam, not as worship from some to others, is the saying of A'sha Bani Tha'labah: "When he came to us after the drowsiness of sleep, / we prostrated to him and raised 'Amar." See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/270.]].

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: its meaning: they fell down prostrate to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, before Joseph [[Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: He raised his parents upon the couch, and they prostrated to him, and his brothers prostrated to him. This contradicts what al-Baghawi mentioned. Al-Naqqash said: This is an error; the pronoun refers back to Joseph, peace be upon him, because of the Most High's saying at the beginning of the surah: (I saw them prostrating to me), and their greeting was that the lowly prostrate to the noble, and the young to the elder. See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/269; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/264.]]. The first is more correct [[The exegetes agreed that that prostration, in whatever manner it was, was only a greeting, not worship. Qatadah said: This was the greeting of kings among them, and Allah gave this community the greeting of the people of Paradise, peace. Al-Qurtubi observed that this abrogated practice had become a custom in his time among some people, so he censured them, saying: "This bowing and bending which has been abrogated for us has become a custom in the land of Egypt and among the non-Arabs, and likewise standing for one another; so that if one of them does not stand for another, he feels in himself as if he is not regarded and has no worth; and likewise when they meet, some of them bow to others, a continuous custom and a settled inheritance, especially when rulers and leaders meet. They have turned away from the sunnah and have deviated from the sunnah." It is related that Anas ibn Malik said: We said: O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)! Should some of us bow to others when we meet? He said: No. We said: Should some of us embrace others? He said: No. We said: Should some of us shake hands with others? He said: Yes (narrated by Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Tamhid). See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/265-266; cf. al-Muharrar al-Wajiz: 8/80; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/491-492.]].

﴿وَقَالَ﴾ Joseph, at that moment: ﴿يَا أَبَتِ هَذَا تَأْوِيلُ رُؤْيَايَ مِنْ قَبْلُ قَدْ جَعَلَهَا رَبِّي حَقًّا﴾ *"O my father! This is the interpretation of my dream from before; my Lord has made it true."* This is His saying: "Indeed I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."

﴿وَقَدْ أَحْسَنَ بِي﴾ *"And He was indeed good to me"* [my Lord, i.e.] [[Omitted from "A".]]: He bestowed favour upon me. ﴿إِذْ أَخْرَجَنِي مِنَ السِّجْنِ﴾ *"when He brought me out of the prison."* He did not say "out of the well" (al-jubb), although the well was a greater trial than the prison, out of courtesy (istikhdaman lil-karam), so that his brothers would not be ashamed after he had said to them: "No reproach upon you today." Also, because Allah's blessing upon him in bringing him out of prison was greater: after coming out of the well he went into slavery and bondage, and after coming out of prison he came to kingship. Also, because his falling into the well was due to the envy of his brothers, whereas in prison it was a recompense from Allah the Most High for a slip that had come from him.

﴿وَجَاءَ بِكُمْ مِنَ الْبَدْوِ﴾ *"and brought you from the desert."* Al-badw is a flat expanse of land inhabited by the people of livestock with their herds; they were people of the desert and of livestock. It is said: badā yabdū, when one goes out to the desert.

﴿مِنْ بَعْدِ أَنْ نَزَغَ﴾ *"after Satan had sown discord"* afsada (corrupted), ﴿الشَّيْطَانُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ إِخْوَتِي﴾ *"between me and my brothers"* through envy.

﴿إِنَّ رَبِّي لَطِيفٌ﴾ *"Indeed my Lord is Gentle"* ayy: possessor of gentleness, ﴿لِمَا يَشَاءُ﴾ *"toward whom He wills."* It was also said: its meaning is "to whomever He wills" [[In "B": li-man.]].

The reality of al-latif (the Gentle) is the One who conveys kindness to others with gentleness (bi'l-rifq) [[In "B": "that He conveys."]]. ﴿إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْعَلِيمُ الْحَكِيمُ﴾ *"Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."*

The historians (ahl al-tarikh) said: Ya'qub remained in Egypt with Joseph for twenty-four years, in the most enviable condition and the most pleasant life. Then he died in Egypt. When death came to him, he bequeathed to his son Joseph that he should carry his body until he buried him beside his father Ishaq. So Joseph did that, and went with him until he buried him in al-Sham (Syria), then he returned to Egypt.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, was carried in a coffin of teak to Bayt al-Maqdis, and that day coincided with the day on which al-Is died, and they were buried in one grave. They had been born in one womb, and their lifespan was one hundred and forty-seven years [[These reports are taken from the People of the Book, and historians have mentioned them together with other reports, and Allah knows best their soundness. The hafiz Ibn Kathir indicated this, indeed he said: "And among the People of the Book it is said that the age of Ya'qub ..." etc. See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/276; Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/363-364; al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya of Ibn Kathir: 1/220; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/492; al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti: 4/589-590.]].

When Allah the Most High had gathered Joseph's scattered family together, and he knew that the bounties of this world do not last, he asked Allah the Most High for a good end, and he said:

﴿My Lord, You have indeed given me of the kingdom﴾: i.e., the kingship of Egypt. Al-mulk (kingship) is the extent of what one is empowered to do for those who hold political authority and administration.

﴿And You taught me of the interpretation of events﴾: i.e., the interpretation of dreams.

﴿Originator (fatir) of the heavens and the earth﴾: i.e., O Originator (fatir) of the heavens and the earth, that is, their Creator. ﴿You are my Protector in this world and the Hereafter﴾: i.e., my Helper and the one who manages my affairs. ﴿Cause me to die in submission (musliman)﴾: he says, take me to You in submission. ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾: he means with my forefathers, the prophets.

Qatadah said: No prophet among the prophets asked for death except Yusuf [[This is also narrated from Ibn Abbas: see al-Durr al-Manthur: 4/591, and see what Ibn Kathir wrote in his Tafsir: 2/493.]].

And regarding the story: when Allah reunited his family and brought his parents and household to him, he longed for his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and said this statement.

Al-Hasan said: He lived many years after this. Others said: When he uttered this statement, a week had not passed before he died.

They differed about the length of Yusuf's absence from his father. Al-Kalbi said: twenty-two years.

It was also said: forty years.

Al-Hasan said: Yusuf was thrown into the well when he was seventeen years old, he was absent from his father for eighty years, he lived after his reunion with Ya'qub for twenty-three years, and he died at the age of one hundred and twenty.

In the Tawrah (Torah, i.e., the Law of Moses as preserved in the Jewish scriptures) it is said that he died at the age of one hundred and ten years, and that Yusuf had three sons from the wife of al-Aziz: Ifra'im, Misha, and Rahmah, who was the wife of Ayyub (Job), the afflicted, peace be upon him.

It was also said: Yusuf lived sixty years after his father. It was said: more. The reports differ concerning this.

He died at the age of one hundred and twenty. They buried him in the Nile in a chest of marble. This was because, when he died, the people competed over him: the people of each quarter asked that he be buried in their quarter, hoping for his blessing, until they nearly came to fighting. So they decided to bury him in the Nile at the point where the water divides in Egypt, so that the water would flow over him and his blessing would reach all of them.

Ikrimah said: He was buried on the right bank of the Nile, and that bank became fertile while the other bank became barren. So he was moved to the left bank, and that bank became fertile while the other bank became barren. Then they buried him in its middle and fixed him in place with a chain, and both banks became fertile together until Musa (Moses) took him out and buried him near his forefathers in al-Sham (Syria) [[See the previous references.]].

**﴿That﴾**, which I have mentioned, **﴿is among the reports of the unseen which We reveal to you. And you were not with them﴾**, meaning: you were not, O Muhammad, with the sons of Ya'qub, **﴿when they resolved upon their plan﴾**, meaning: when they determined to throw Yusuf into the well, **﴿while they were scheming﴾** against Yusuf.

**﴿And most of mankind, [O Muhammad], will not be believers, even if you should strive eagerly﴾** for their faith.

It is narrated that the Jews and the Quraysh asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the story of Yusuf. When he informed them of it in accordance with the Torah, they did not accept Islam, and the Prophet (ﷺ) grieved. So it was said to him: "Indeed they will not believe, even if you strive eagerly for their faith."[[Ibn al-Anbari said: The Quraysh and the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the story of Yusuf and his brothers, and he explained it in a thorough manner, hoping that this would be a cause of their Islam. But they contradicted his expectation, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grieved, and Allah the Exalted consoled him with this verse. See: Zad al-Masir: 4/293; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/350.]]

**﴿That﴾**, which I have mentioned, **﴿is among the reports of the unseen which We reveal to you. And you were not with them﴾**, meaning: you were not, O Muhammad, with the sons of Ya'qub, **﴿when they resolved upon their plan﴾**, meaning: when they determined to throw Yusuf into the well, **﴿while they were scheming﴾** against Yusuf.

**﴿And most of mankind, [O Muhammad], will not be believers, even if you should strive eagerly﴾** for their faith.

It is narrated that the Jews and the Quraysh asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the story of Yusuf. When he informed them of it in accordance with the Torah, they did not accept Islam, and the Prophet (ﷺ) grieved. So it was said to him: "Indeed they will not believe, even if you strive eagerly for their faith."[[Ibn al-Anbari said: The Quraysh and the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the story of Yusuf and his brothers, and he explained it in a thorough manner, hoping that this would be a cause of their Islam. But they contradicted his expectation, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grieved, and Allah the Exalted consoled him with this verse. See: Zad al-Masir: 4/293; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/350.]]

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verses 104–106:**

﴿And you do not ask them for any reward for it﴾, meaning, for conveying the message and calling to God, the Exalted, ﴿any wage﴾ (*ju'l*, a payment for something done or said; its verbal noun is *ja'l*, and it means the fee given for a thing, whether an act or a statement; see Ibn al-Athir, *al-Nihayah*, 1/276; al-Qunawi, *Anis al-Fuqaha'*, p. 169) ﴿or recompense﴾. ﴿It is not but a reminder﴾, meaning the Qur'an is ﴿not but a reminder﴾, an admonition and a warning ﴿to the worlds﴾.

﴿And how many a sign﴾, meaning how many, ﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾, a lesson and a proof, ﴿do they pass by, while they turn away from it﴾, not reflecting upon it and not taking heed from it.

﴿And most of them do not believe in God except while they are associates [with Him]﴾. Their belief was such that when they were asked, "Who created the heavens and the earth?", they said, "God." And when it was said to them, "Who sends down the rain?", they said, "God." Yet despite that, they worshipped idols and associated [others with God] (this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Sha'bi, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd; see al-Tabari, *Tafsir*, 16/286–288; Ibn Kathir, 2/495; al-Suyuti, *al-Durr al-Manthur*, 4/593).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "It was revealed concerning the *talbiyah* (the chant of the pagan Arabs during the pilgrimage). They used to say in their *talbiyah*: 'Here I am, O God, here I am. Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours; You own him and what he owns.'" (This is established in the two Sahihs. In Sahih Muslim (2/843) it is related that when they said, "Here I am, You have no partner," the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, "Woe to you, enough, enough!" (meaning: be content and do not add to this). But they would say, "Except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns." However, these hadiths do not mention that the verses were revealed concerning this. Rather, it is a description of their state in the Jahiliyyah and their *talbiyah*. See also Ibn Kathir, 2/495.)

'Ata' said: "This refers to supplication (*du'a'*), because the disbelievers forgot their Lord in times of ease, but when affliction befell them, they became sincere in their supplication." (See al-Andalusi, *al-Bahr al-Muhit*, 5/351. All of the reports mentioned above and others are included within the general meaning of this noble verse and do not contradict one another, for all of that was actually done by them, and the verse describes all of it.)

As God, the Exalted, says: ﴿And they thought that they were encompassed by it, they called upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Yunus: 22], and God, the Exalted, says: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, at once they associate [others with Him]﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65], and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 107–108:

﴿Do they feel secure that there will not come upon them an overwhelming punishment from Allah?﴾ That is: a covering punishment. Mujahid said: "A punishment that will envelop them." Its parallel is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿On the Day the punishment will envelop them from above them﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:55], and so on. Qatadah said: "A calamity (waqi'ah)." al-Dahhak said: "It means the thunderbolts and the calamities."

﴿Or the Hour will come upon them suddenly﴾ unexpectedly, ﴿while they are unaware﴾ of its coming. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Blast will stir people while they are in their markets."

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿This is my way﴾: this is the call to which I call and the path upon which I am, ﴿my way (sabili)﴾ meaning my sunnah (practice) and my method (minhaj). Muqatil said: "My religion." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾ [al-Nahl 16:125], meaning: to His religion.

﴿I invite to Allah with insight﴾ with certainty. And "insight" (basirah) is the knowledge by which one distinguishes between truth and falsehood. ﴿I and whoever follows me﴾ meaning: whoever believes in me and affirms me also invites to Allah. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd, who said: "It is incumbent upon whoever follows him to call to what he called to, and to remind with the Qur'an." [[See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/293. The call to Allah is the call to belief in Him and in what His messengers brought, by affirming what they reported and obeying what they commanded; this includes calling to the two testimonies, establishing the prayer, paying the zakat, fasting Ramadan, performing the Hajj to the House, calling to belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, resurrection after death, and belief in divine decree, both its good and its evil, and calling the servant to worship his Lord as if he sees Him. These three levels, "Islam," "iman" and "ihsan," are included in the religion, as he said in the authentic hadith: "This is Jibril; he came to you to teach you your religion," after he had answered him concerning these three... So the call to Allah is by calling the servant to His religion, and its foundation is worshipping Him alone without partner, as Allah sent His messengers with this and revealed His books with it... The messengers agree upon the religion that comprises the foundations of belief and practice. The Messenger ﷺ carried out this call to Allah, and it is by His permission, glory be to Him; he did not legislate a religion that Allah had not permitted. Among what clarifies this: He, glory be to Him, mentions that He commanded him to call to Allah at times, and at other times to call to His way, since it is known that the caller who invites others to a matter must, in what he invites to, have two things: the first is the intended goal, and the second is the means and path leading to the goal. Therefore He mentions calling sometimes to Allah and sometimes to His way, for He, glory be to Him, is the worshipped One who is the intended object of the call. See: Daqa'iq al-Tafsir, Ibn Taymiyyah: 3/284 and following.]].

It was said: the speech is complete at His saying ﴿I invite to Allah﴾, then He resumes: ﴿with insight, I and whoever follows me﴾, meaning: I am upon insight from my Lord, and so is everyone who follows me.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means the companions of Muhammad ﷺ, who were upon the best way and the most upright guidance, the source of knowledge, the treasure of faith, and the army of the Most Merciful."

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "Whoever would follow, let him follow those who have passed away [for the living is not safe from temptation]. They are the companions of Muhammad ﷺ, the best of this Ummah, the purest of hearts, the deepest in knowledge, and the least in affectation, a people whom Allah chose to accompany His Prophet ﷺ and to establish His religion. [So recognize their virtue, follow their footsteps, and hold fast to what you can of their character and conduct], for they were upon the straight guidance." [[A statement from Ibn Mas'ud, narrated by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad (5/211), edited by Shaykh Ahmad Shakir. al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (1/178): "Narrated by Ahmad, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, and its narrators are trustworthy."]]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Glory be to Allah﴾, meaning: say, "Glory be to Allah," declaring Him far above what they associate with Him.

﴿And I am not of the polytheists.﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 107–108:

﴿Do they feel secure that there will not come upon them an overwhelming punishment from Allah?﴾ That is: a covering punishment. Mujahid said: "A punishment that will envelop them." Its parallel is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿On the Day the punishment will envelop them from above them﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:55], and so on. Qatadah said: "A calamity (waqi'ah)." al-Dahhak said: "It means the thunderbolts and the calamities."

﴿Or the Hour will come upon them suddenly﴾ unexpectedly, ﴿while they are unaware﴾ of its coming. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Blast will stir people while they are in their markets."

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿This is my way﴾: this is the call to which I call and the path upon which I am, ﴿my way (sabili)﴾ meaning my sunnah (practice) and my method (minhaj). Muqatil said: "My religion." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾ [al-Nahl 16:125], meaning: to His religion.

﴿I invite to Allah with insight﴾ with certainty. And "insight" (basirah) is the knowledge by which one distinguishes between truth and falsehood. ﴿I and whoever follows me﴾ meaning: whoever believes in me and affirms me also invites to Allah. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd, who said: "It is incumbent upon whoever follows him to call to what he called to, and to remind with the Qur'an." [[See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/293. The call to Allah is the call to belief in Him and in what His messengers brought, by affirming what they reported and obeying what they commanded; this includes calling to the two testimonies, establishing the prayer, paying the zakat, fasting Ramadan, performing the Hajj to the House, calling to belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, resurrection after death, and belief in divine decree, both its good and its evil, and calling the servant to worship his Lord as if he sees Him. These three levels, "Islam," "iman" and "ihsan," are included in the religion, as he said in the authentic hadith: "This is Jibril; he came to you to teach you your religion," after he had answered him concerning these three... So the call to Allah is by calling the servant to His religion, and its foundation is worshipping Him alone without partner, as Allah sent His messengers with this and revealed His books with it... The messengers agree upon the religion that comprises the foundations of belief and practice. The Messenger ﷺ carried out this call to Allah, and it is by His permission, glory be to Him; he did not legislate a religion that Allah had not permitted. Among what clarifies this: He, glory be to Him, mentions that He commanded him to call to Allah at times, and at other times to call to His way, since it is known that the caller who invites others to a matter must, in what he invites to, have two things: the first is the intended goal, and the second is the means and path leading to the goal. Therefore He mentions calling sometimes to Allah and sometimes to His way, for He, glory be to Him, is the worshipped One who is the intended object of the call. See: Daqa'iq al-Tafsir, Ibn Taymiyyah: 3/284 and following.]].

It was said: the speech is complete at His saying ﴿I invite to Allah﴾, then He resumes: ﴿with insight, I and whoever follows me﴾, meaning: I am upon insight from my Lord, and so is everyone who follows me.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means the companions of Muhammad ﷺ, who were upon the best way and the most upright guidance, the source of knowledge, the treasure of faith, and the army of the Most Merciful."

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "Whoever would follow, let him follow those who have passed away [for the living is not safe from temptation]. They are the companions of Muhammad ﷺ, the best of this Ummah, the purest of hearts, the deepest in knowledge, and the least in affectation, a people whom Allah chose to accompany His Prophet ﷺ and to establish His religion. [So recognize their virtue, follow their footsteps, and hold fast to what you can of their character and conduct], for they were upon the straight guidance." [[A statement from Ibn Mas'ud, narrated by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad (5/211), edited by Shaykh Ahmad Shakir. al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (1/178): "Narrated by Ahmad, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, and its narrators are trustworthy."]]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Glory be to Allah﴾, meaning: say, "Glory be to Allah," declaring Him far above what they associate with Him.

﴿And I am not of the polytheists.﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 109:

﴿And We sent not before you [O Muhammad] except men﴾, not angels, ﴿to whom We revealed﴾. Hafs recited ﴿nūḥī﴾ with the nūn and a kasra on the ḥā’, while the others recited it with the yā’ and a fatḥa on the ḥā’.

﴿from among the people of the towns﴾, meaning: from among the people of the cities (amsar), not the nomadic dwellers of the desert (al-bawadi), because the people of the cities are more intelligent, more virtuous, more knowledgeable, and more forbearing.

[Al-Hasan said: Allah did not send a prophet from among the desert dwellers, nor from among the jinn, nor from among women. And it was said: He only did not send [a prophet] from among the people of the desert because of their harshness and rudeness.] [[What is between the brackets is omitted from "b".]]

﴿Have they not travelled through the earth﴾, meaning: these polytheists who deny, ﴿and seen how was the end﴾, the final outcome of affairs, ﴿of those before them﴾, meaning: the nations who denied, so that they may take heed.

﴿And the Abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are God-fearing﴾. He, mighty is His remembrance, says: this is Our practice with the people of Our allegiance and obedience, that We deliver them when the punishment descends, and what is in the Abode of the Hereafter is better for them. He omitted what we have mentioned, being satisfied with what the context indicates about it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Abode of the Hereafter﴾. It was said: its meaning is "and the Abode of the state of the Hereafter."

And it was said: this is the attribution of a thing to itself, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95], and like their saying: "the day of Thursday" and "Rabi' al-Akhir" (the latter Rabi').

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾, so that you would believe.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 110:

﴿Until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied, Our help came to them﴾ The readers differed concerning His words: ﴿kudhibu﴾ (they had been denied).

The people of Kufa and Abu Ja'far recited ﴿kudhibu﴾ with light emphasis (takhfif), and ʿĀ'isha used to disapprove of this reading [[Al-Bukhari narrated in the Tafsir of Surah Yusuf (8/367), from Ibn Shihab who said: ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr informed me, from ʿĀ'isha -may Allah be pleased with her- that when he asked her about the words of Allah the Exalted, "Until, when the messengers despaired," he said: I said: Is it "akdhabu" or "kudhibu"? ʿĀ'isha said: "Kudhibu." I said: Then they were certain that their people had denied them, so it is not assumption. She said: Indeed, by my life, they were certain of that. I said to her: "And they thought that they had been denied"? She said: Allah forbid, the messengers would never think such a thing about their Lord. I said: Then what is this verse? She said: They are the followers of the messengers who believed in their Lord and affirmed them; the trial lengthened upon them and the help was delayed from them, until the messengers despaired of those among their people who denied them, and the messengers thought that their followers had denied them; then the help of Allah came at that time." This reading is the reading of the majority, and al-Tabari supported it in his Tafsir: 16/309.]].

The others recited it with emphasis (tashdid).

Whoever recited with emphasis said: its meaning is: until the messengers despaired of the faith of their people.

[It is narrated from Mujahid that he recited: ﴿wa-qad kadhabu﴾ with a fatha on the kaf and the dhal lightened, and it has two interpretations: one of them is that the idolatrous people thought that the messengers had lied. The second is that the messengers thought -that is, knew- that their people had fabricated against Allah in their disbelief, concerning the faith of their people.]

"And they thought" means: that is, the messengers were certain that the nations had denied them with a denial after which their faith was not hoped for.

Assumption (zann) in the sense of certainty (yaqin): this is the meaning of Qatada's statement.

Some of them said: its meaning is: until the messengers despaired that those among their people who denied them would affirm them, and they thought that those among their people who had believed in them had denied them and turned back from their religion, due to the severity of the trial and affliction upon them and the delay of help. Whoever recited with lightening said: its meaning is: until the messengers despaired of the faith of their people, and "they thought," that is, their people thought that the messengers had lied to them concerning the threat of punishment.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: its meaning is the weakness of the hearts of the messengers, that is: the messengers thought that they had lied concerning the help they had promised. They were human, so they weakened and despaired and thought that they had been broken with. Then he recited: ﴿Until the Messenger and those who believed with him say: When is the help of Allah?﴾ [Al-Baqara: 214], that is: Our help came to the messengers.

[On the grammatical and interpretive discussion of the two readings and weighing between them, see: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/296-311, al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/354-355, Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/498-499, Daqa'iq al-Tafsir by Ibn Taymiyya: 3/301 onward.]].

﴿So whom We will is rescued﴾ [The common readers recited with two nuns, that is: We rescue whom We will] [[Omitted from "a".]]. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, ʿAsim and Ya'qub recited with a single nun, pronounced with a damma and the jim emphasized, with a fatha on the ya in the passive form (ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu), because it is written in the Mushaf with a single nun; so the position of ﴿man﴾ is nominative (raf') according to this reading. According to the first reading it is accusative (nasb): so whom We will is rescued at the descent of the punishment, and they are the believers who obey.

﴿And His punishment is not turned back﴾ [ba'suna: Our punishment] ﴿from the guilty people﴾ [i.e.: the idolaters].

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 111:

﴿Indeed, in their stories﴾ 188/a: that is, in the account of Yusuf (Joseph) and his brothers, ﴿there is a lesson﴾, an admonition, ﴿for those of understanding.﴾ ﴿It was not a narration invented﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿that is fabricated﴾, i.e., invented. ﴿Rather, it is a confirmation of what was﴾, i.e., rather it was a confirmation of what was ﴿before it﴾ of the Tawrah (Torah) and the Injil (Gospel), ﴿and a detailed explanation of all things﴾ that the servants need of the lawful and the unlawful, the commands and the prohibitions, ﴿and guidance and mercy﴾, a clarification and a blessing, ﴿for a people who believe.﴾
